days.title: Doctrine 4, Day 2: Biblical Development
days.content:
### Creation and the Image of God in the Law

The Pentateuch establishes the doctrine of man with unusual care, devoting two full chapters of Genesis to the subject before the narrative of the fall even begins. Genesis 1 situates man's creation as the climactic, final act of the six creative days, distinguished from every other creature by the phrase "in our image, after our likeness" (Genesis 1:26) — a phrase used nowhere else in the creation account. The plural "us" and "our," read in light of the full biblical revelation of the Trinity, signals that man's creation involved deliberation within the Godhead itself, a dignity granted to no other creature in the six days of creation.

Genesis 2 then narrates the same creation from a different vantage, with attention to man's formation from the dust and the breath of God, his placement in a prepared garden with meaningful work to do (Genesis 2:15), his naming of the animals as an exercise of delegated authority (Genesis 2:19-20), and finally the creation of woman from man's own side, "bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh" (Genesis 2:23), establishing both her full equality in nature and dignity with the man and the one-flesh union of marriage (Genesis 2:24).

The dominion mandate given in Genesis 1:28 is not incidental to the doctrine of man but central to it. Man is not merely placed within creation as one more inhabitant; he is placed over creation as God's appointed steward, ruling the created order on God's behalf and under God's authority. This is dominion under God, not independence from Him — man rules creation as a delegated vice-regent, not as an autonomous sovereign. This distinction matters: human dignity is derivative, not self-generated. Man's authority over creation exists only because God first granted it.

### Reason, Language, and Creativity as Marks of the Image

Part of what it means for man to bear God's image is reflected in capacities given to no other earthly creature — reasoned thought, articulate language, and creative work. God Himself speaks creation into being ("And God said," Genesis 1:3, and throughout the chapter), and His image-bearer is given a corresponding capacity for speech, immediately exercised in the naming of the animals (Genesis 2:19-20), an act requiring observation, categorization, and language — the exercise of a mind capable of ordered thought. This capacity is not incidental; it is part of what distinguishes man from every other creature God made "after his kind" (Genesis 1:24-25) but not after His own image.

Genesis also records the early flowering of human creativity — Jubal, "the father of all such as handle the harp and organ," and Tubal-cain, an "instructer of every artificer in brass and iron" (Genesis 4:21-22). Even in a genealogy marked by the spread of sin, this note of creative capacity persists, evidence that the image of God, though marred, is not erased; man continues to reflect, however imperfectly, the Maker who Himself creates, orders, and delights in beauty. This capacity for reasoned thought, meaningful language, and purposeful creativity remains, throughout Scripture, a mark distinguishing man from the rest of the created order and a further expression of what it means to bear God's likeness.

### Community and the Image of a Relational God

Before sin ever entered the world, God pronounced one thing about His finished creation "not good": "It is not good that the man should be alone" (Genesis 2:18). This is a striking statement placed within an otherwise unbroken sequence of divine approval. Man was made, from the very beginning, for relationship — with God first, and with his fellow image-bearer as well. This reflects something of the very nature of the God in whose image man is made. The plural counsel of Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man," read in light of the Trinity's full revelation, suggests that man's capacity for relationship mirrors, however distantly, the eternal relationship within the Godhead itself — Father, Son, and Spirit, one in essence, ever in relation. Man, made in that image, is therefore not designed for isolated self-sufficiency but for communion — with his Maker, with his spouse, and within the wider human family. This is part of the reason Scripture treats isolation and estrangement as a wound to be healed, not a neutral state to be accepted, and why the church, as a gathered community rather than a collection of solitary individuals, corresponds so fittingly to what man was made to be.

### Man's Capacity for Covenant

Among the capacities unique to man as God's image-bearer is the ability to enter binding, covenantal relationship with his Maker — a capacity given to no other creature in the created order. God establishes covenant with Noah after the flood, binding Himself by promise and giving a sign, the rainbow, as its perpetual reminder (Genesis 9:9-13). He establishes covenant with Abraham, promising land, descendants, and blessing to all nations through him, and binding that promise with a solemn covenant ceremony (Genesis 15:18; 17:7). Later, at Sinai, He establishes covenant with the whole nation of Israel, a covenant sealed with sacrificial blood and received by the people's own sworn response: "All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient" (Exodus 24:7-8). This capacity for covenant — the ability to receive promises, make vows, and enter binding relationship with the eternal God — is itself a further expression of what it means to be made in His image, a rational and moral agent capable of relationship with his Maker that no other creature shares. It reaches its fullest expression in the new covenant, "not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers... but this shall be the covenant that I will make... I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts" (Jeremiah 31:32-33), the covenant Christ inaugurates at the Last Supper and seals with His own blood (Luke 22:20).

### Made for Worship

Among the capacities that distinguish man from the rest of the created order is the capacity — indeed, the design — to know and worship his Maker. No other creature in Scripture is addressed by God, reasoned with by God, or invited into covenant relationship with God as man is. The Psalms are saturated with the assumption that worship is man's native calling, not an optional add-on to his existence: "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker" (Psalm 95:6), and "It is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture" (Psalm 100:3). Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that the Father actively "seeketh" worshippers who will worship Him "in spirit and in truth" (John 4:23) — language that presents worship not as a religious duty man performs to appease a distant deity, but as the very purpose for which man's capacity for relationship with God was designed in the first place. When man withholds worship from His Maker and redirects it elsewhere, as Romans 1 describes, it is not merely a rule broken but a design abandoned — the misuse of the very capacity that most distinguishes him as God's image-bearer.

### The Whole Person Called to Love God

Israel's central confession, recited daily as the heart of covenant devotion, addresses man in his full, undivided constitution: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD: And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might" (Deuteronomy 6:4-5). This command assumes exactly what Genesis 2:7 and 1 Thessalonians 5:23 establish elsewhere in this doctrine — that man is not a collection of separable parts, one of which might be devoted to God while another is withheld, but a single, unified being whose whole self is claimed by his Maker. Jesus affirms this command as the greatest in all the Law, adding the word "mind" to make the totality unmistakable: "with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength" (Mark 12:30). Because man is made whole — body, soul, spirit, mind, and strength together — worship that engages only the intellect, or only the emotions, or only outward ritual, falls short of what the doctrine of man requires. The whole person was made by God, and the whole person is called to love Him in return.

### Man and Woman: Equal Dignity, Distinct Callings

Genesis 1:27 establishes, in a single verse, both the full equality and the deliberate distinction God wove into humanity from the beginning: "male and female created he them." Both bear the image of God fully and equally; the text does not say the man alone bears the image while the woman merely assists him. Genesis 2 supplies the manner of the woman's creation, formed from the man's own side while he slept (Genesis 2:21-22) — not from the dust separately, as though she were an afterthought, but from his own body, so that he exclaims, "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh" (Genesis 2:23). Her creation completes rather than supplements his; before her creation, God Himself declares the man's aloneness "not good" (Genesis 2:18), the only thing in the whole created order so described before the Fall.

Scripture holds together, without contradiction, the equal dignity of man and woman and the distinct callings God gives to each within marriage and the family. Paul instructs husbands to love their wives "even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it" (Ephesians 5:25) — a headship defined by sacrificial love, not domination — while wives are called to respect that headship as the church honors Christ (Ephesians 5:22-24, 33). Peter likewise instructs husbands to dwell with their wives "according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life" (1 Peter 3:7) — a striking phrase that grounds marital honor directly in the wife's equal share in the grace of eternal life. Whatever distinct roles Scripture assigns within marriage and the church, it never suggests that woman is in any way a lesser image-bearer than man; both stand before God as "heirs together" of the very same grace.

Paul takes the doctrine of marriage a step further still, revealing that the one-flesh union established in Genesis 2 was never merely a social institution but a living picture of a greater reality. After quoting Genesis 2:24 directly, he adds, "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church" (Ephesians 5:31-32). Marriage between man and woman, in other words, was designed from the beginning to portray, however dimly, the covenant love between Christ and His redeemed people — the husband's sacrificial headship echoing Christ's self-giving love, the wife's responsive love echoing the church's devotion to her Lord. This is a striking development in the doctrine of Anthropology: the most basic human relationship God instituted at creation was, even then, already pointing forward to the gospel that would one day be preached in its fullest form.

The Law continues to affirm this doctrine even after the fall. Genesis 9:6, given to Noah after the flood, grounds the prohibition of murder directly in the doctrine of the image of God: "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man" (Genesis 9:6). This is a critical development — even after sin has entered the world and marred humanity, Scripture does not say the image of God has been erased. It remains the very basis for the sanctity of human life and the gravity of taking it. The Mosaic law that follows continues to treat every Israelite, regardless of social standing, as possessing inherent worth before God, evident in laws protecting the poor, the sojourner, the widow, and the orphan (Exodus 22:21-22; Deuteronomy 24:17-18) — provisions that make sense only if every human being carries dignity that must be honored, not earned.

The Law also establishes that the image of God is not a quality lost after one generation but a nature transmitted to every descendant of Adam. Genesis 5:1-3 deliberately echoes the language of Genesis 1: "In the day that God created man, in the likeness of God made he him... And Adam... begat a son in his own likeness, after his image." The text draws a direct parallel — as God made Adam in His own image and likeness, so Adam fathers Seth in Adam's own image and likeness. This is a crucial development: the image of God is not confined to the first couple but is the inherited constitution of the entire human race, passed on to every generation, even a fallen one. Every human being who has ever lived, without exception, bears this inheritance.

The Law further reveals man's created purpose through the rhythm it establishes for human life. The Sabbath command — "the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work" (Exodus 20:10) — is grounded explicitly in the pattern of creation itself: God rested on the seventh day and blessed it (Genesis 2:2-3). Man, made in God's image, is given the same rhythm of labor and rest that marks his Maker's own pattern of work. This is not incidental; it reveals that man was made for more than ceaseless productivity. His worth is not measured only by output, since even in his God-given work he is called to cease, trust, and worship — a dignity that resists every system, ancient or modern, that would reduce a human being to the value of his labor.

### The Blessing of Multiplication and the Family

The dominion mandate of Genesis 1:28 begins not with subduing the earth but with a blessing of fruitfulness: "Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth." Family and generational increase are, from the very first chapter of Scripture, presented as a good gift bound up with man's created purpose, not a burden to be minimized or an afterthought to dominion. The Psalms celebrate children as a heritage from the Lord rather than a private accomplishment of the parents who bear them: "Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward" (Psalm 127:3), and the same psalm compares a household full of children to a quiver full of arrows, a source of strength and blessing rather than mere expense (Psalm 127:4-5). The prophet Malachi, confronting a generation careless with marriage covenants, asks pointedly why God made husband and wife one: "that he might seek a godly seed" (Malachi 2:15) — the family is not merely a private arrangement but the ordained context in which the next generation is to be raised to know and serve the Lord.

This purpose continues explicitly into the Law's instruction for covenant parents. Moses commands Israel to teach God's words diligently to their children, speaking of them at home, on the road, at rising and at lying down (Deuteronomy 6:6-7) — the family is the primary institution through which the knowledge of God is to be transmitted across generations, prior to and alongside any other institution. The wisdom literature reinforces the same charge: "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it" (Proverbs 22:6). Human dignity, established in Anthropology's opening claim, is therefore not merely an individual possession but a trust to be handed down — every generation of image-bearers charged with raising the next to know the God whose image they carry.

### Original Righteousness and the Goodness of Man's Creation

Genesis 1:31 closes the creation account with God's own verdict on His finished work, man included: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." This is a deliberate escalation from the repeated "good" pronounced over the earlier days of creation (Genesis 1:4, 10, 12, 18, 21, 25) — with man's creation, the whole work reaches "very good," its highest commendation. Man was not created flawed, morally neutral, or merely capable of goodness; he was created upright. Solomon states this directly, centuries later, even while surveying humanity's corruption: "Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions" (Ecclesiastes 7:29). This verse is a critical hinge for the whole doctrine of man: it affirms both original righteousness (God made man upright) and the reality that followed (man's own inventions departed from that uprightness) — establishing, in one sentence, both the goodness of God's original design and the seriousness of humanity's later fall from it, the very hinge on which the next doctrine in this chapter turns.

### Human Dignity as the Ground of Justice

Because Genesis 9:6 grounds the penalty for murder directly in man's bearing of God's image, the doctrine of Anthropology becomes the foundation for the entire biblical concept of justice. Governing authority itself is later described by Paul as instituted by God partly for this very purpose — to restrain wrongdoing against fellow image-bearers and to uphold the good: "he is the minister of God to thee for good... he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil" (Romans 13:4). Justice, in this framework, is not an arbitrary social construct but a response owed to beings of inherent worth; a society's treatment of the vulnerable — the poor, the oppressed, the falsely accused — becomes, in Scripture, a direct index of whether it honors or dishonors the image of God its members bear. The prophets repeatedly indict Israel not merely for false worship but for injustice toward fellow image-bearers: "Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow" (Isaiah 1:17). Anthropology, rightly understood, is never merely personal piety; it has direct bearing on how a community structures its treatment of every member within it.

### Man's Distinctiveness from the Animal Creation

Genesis 1 itself draws a careful distinction: every other living creature is made "after his kind" (Genesis 1:21, 24-25), a phrase never once applied to man, who alone is made "in our image, after our likeness" (Genesis 1:26). This distinction is not incidental. The Writings occasionally press this distinctiveness by way of sobering comparison — the psalmist observes that a man without understanding, who trusts in his own wealth rather than God, "is like the beasts that perish" (Psalm 49:12, 20), a warning, not a description of man's created nature, aimed at those who squander the very capacities that set them apart. Ecclesiastes, in one of its most searching passages, observes that man and beast share the same breath and the same end in physical death, "so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for all is vanity" (Ecclesiastes 3:19) — yet immediately follows this sober observation with a question that reopens the very distinction just questioned: "Who knoweth the spirit of man that goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast that goeth downward to the earth?" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). Read within the whole canon rather than in isolation, Ecclesiastes here voices the honest bewilderment of life "under the sun," while the rest of Scripture answers its own question plainly: man's spirit does indeed go upward, to give account before the God in whose image he was made, and no such destiny is ever ascribed to the animal creation.

### Man's Dignity in the Writings and Prophets

The Psalms return repeatedly to the wonder of human dignity as God's handiwork. Psalm 139 reflects on this with unmatched intimacy: "For thou hast possessed my reins: thou hast covered me in my mother's womb. I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well" (Psalm 139:13-14). This text extends the doctrine of the image of God to the individual, unborn person — each human life, from its earliest formation, is a deliberate, personal work of God, not an accident of biology.

Ecclesiastes, for all its meditation on the vanity of life under the sun, never abandons the conviction that man is made for something beyond mere existence — that God "hath set the world in their heart" (Ecclesiastes 3:11), a longing for eternity that marks humanity as distinct from the animals, even amid the frustrations of a fallen world. The wisdom literature as a whole treats human beings as reasoning, morally accountable agents capable of receiving instruction, exercising judgment, and choosing between wisdom and folly — a dignity of moral agency assumed throughout Proverbs.

The prophets, even while pronouncing judgment on human sin, never lose sight of humanity's created worth. Isaiah contrasts the frailty of man's flesh with God's eternal word — "All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field" (Isaiah 40:6) — yet the same prophet speaks of God forming, making, and calling His people by name with tender particularity (Isaiah 43:1). Jeremiah records God's word concerning his own formation: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee" (Jeremiah 1:5), extending the doctrine of God's deliberate, personal formation of individual human life beyond the patriarchal narratives into the prophetic office itself.

The book of Job, more than any other Old Testament book, wrestles honestly with the apparent gap between man's exalted dignity and his frequent suffering, yet even there the doctrine holds firm. Job appeals to the very fact of his creation as grounds for God's care: "Thine hands have made me and fashioned me together round about; yet thou dost destroy me... Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay" (Job 10:8-9). Elihu adds his own testimony to the same doctrine: "The spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life" (Job 33:4). Job's dignity is never in question in the book that bears his name — what is in question is how a good God governs a world where dignified image-bearers suffer, a tension Job brings honestly before God rather than resolving by lowering his view of either God or man.

### Human Dignity and the Meaning of Work

From the very beginning, God did not place man in the garden to be idle but "to dress it and to keep it" (Genesis 2:15), work given before sin entered the world and therefore no part of the curse itself, though it becomes toilsome after the Fall (Genesis 3:17-19). Man's dignity as image-bearer is expressed, in part, through meaningful labor — not as a necessary evil to be endured but as a genuine expression of the dominion mandate, an extension of God's own creative and ordering work into the world He entrusted to man's care. Ecclesiastes, despite its sober assessment of labor's frustrations under the sun, still commends work as a gift: "There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour" (Ecclesiastes 2:24). Paul continues this theme into the New Testament, instructing believers to labor "with their own hands the thing which is good" (Ephesians 4:28) and warning that unwillingness to work is itself a departure from the created pattern of human dignity through purposeful labor (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Work, rightly understood, is not opposed to human dignity but is one of its natural expressions.

### The Image of God Across the Span of Life

Scripture consistently affirms the full dignity of the image of God at every stage of human life, refusing to make personhood contingent on age, ability, or independence. The unborn are treated throughout Scripture not as potential persons but as persons already known and valued by God — Jeremiah was known and sanctified by God before he was formed in the womb (Jeremiah 1:5), David was fearfully and wonderfully made while still unformed (Psalm 139:13-16), and even in the Gospels, the unborn John the Baptist leaps for joy in his mother's womb at the presence of the unborn Christ (Luke 1:41, 44) — an encounter between two persons, not two potential persons. Children, though weak and dependent, are received by Christ with particular tenderness: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God" (Mark 10:14). And the aged, though their strength may fail, are not thereby diminished in worth; the psalmist prays, "Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth" (Psalm 71:9), a plea that assumes continued divine care and honor owed to age rather than discard. The Law commands, "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man" (Leviticus 19:32) — dignity owed to the elderly precisely because of, not despite, their advancing years. From the womb to old age, Scripture presents one unbroken doctrine of human worth, undiminished at either end of life.

### The Two-fold Constitution of Man: Body and Spirit

Scripture consistently presents man as possessing both a material and an immaterial dimension, joined together as a single living person rather than two separate substances loosely attached. Genesis 2:7 already establishes this — dust and breath together become "a living soul," not a soul trapped inside a body it merely inhabits. Ecclesiastes describes death as the dissolution of this unity, when "the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7) — a picture of separation that only makes sense if the two were, in life, joined.

This two-fold constitution grounds man's capacity for relationship with God on one hand and with the physical creation on the other. Jesus Himself affirms both dimensions when He warns, "fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell" (Matthew 10:28) — a statement that assumes the body can be killed while something of the person, the soul, persists beyond that death, awaiting the resurrection. Hebrews 4:12 speaks of the word of God as "quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit," language that presupposes real, though not always sharply separable, distinctions within man's inward being. Whatever precision theologians may debate about the exact relationship of soul and spirit, Scripture is unwavering on the central point: man is not merely a body, and man is not merely a soul trapped in unwanted matter. He is both, together, by God's design — and both together will be raised, redeemed, and glorified.

### Human Dignity in Weakness and Suffering

Because human dignity rests on the image of God rather than on strength, health, or capability, Scripture is able to speak of profound dignity persisting even amid weakness, disability, and suffering. Paul, pleading with God three times to remove a persistent physical affliction, receives instead a different kind of answer: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Far from treating this weakness as a diminishment of his worth or usefulness, Paul concludes, "when I am weak, then am I strong" (2 Corinthians 12:10) — human limitation becomes, in God's economy, not evidence of reduced dignity but the very occasion for God's power to be displayed. Paul elsewhere distinguishes between the "outward man" that perishes and the "inward man" that is renewed day by day, even as the body weakens (2 Corinthians 4:16) — a believer's truest identity and worth are never reducible to physical capacity or decline. This doctrine matters immensely for how the community of faith regards those living with illness, disability, or the frailties of age: not as diminished image-bearers whose worth has lessened, but as image-bearers through whom God's sufficiency is, if anything, more visibly displayed.

### Moral Agency and Accountability

Because man is made in God's image, he is made a reasoning, willing, morally accountable creature — capable of understanding right and wrong, capable of choosing between them, and answerable to his Maker for the choice. This capacity is presupposed from the very first command given in the garden: God does not compel Adam's obedience but sets before him a genuine choice, with genuine consequences (Genesis 2:16-17). Moses later makes this moral agency explicit to the whole nation of Israel: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19). Joshua repeats the same appeal to the nation's will: "choose you this day whom ye will serve" (Joshua 24:15).

This accountability does not diminish after the Fall; if anything, Scripture intensifies it. Ezekiel confronts a generation tempted to blame their fathers for their own sin, insisting that each person bears responsibility for his own choices: "The soul that sinneth, it shall die... the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him" (Ezekiel 18:20). Paul carries this same doctrine into the New Testament, teaching that "every one of us shall give account of himself to God" (Romans 14:12). Man's dignity as a rational, volitional agent — capable of genuine choice rather than mere instinct — is inseparable from his accountability before the God who made him this way. A creature without moral agency could not sin; a creature without dignity could not be held responsible. Scripture presents man as possessing both, together, from the beginning.

### Christ and the Original Order in the Gospels

When questioned about marriage and divorce, Jesus does not appeal to evolving custom or shifting cultural consensus; He appeals directly to the creation account in Genesis as settled, authoritative, and binding: "Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, and said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?" (Matthew 19:4-5). This is significant for the doctrine of Anthropology: Jesus Himself treats the Genesis creation account as historical fact establishing the created order, not as myth or metaphor to be reinterpreted by later generations.

Throughout His earthly ministry, Jesus consistently treats every person He encounters — regardless of gender, ethnicity, social class, ceremonial status, or moral history — as possessing inherent worth deserving of attention, compassion, and dignity. He speaks with the Samaritan woman at the well, in defiance of the social conventions of His day (John 4:7-26). He touches lepers rather than merely healing them from a distance (Mark 1:41). He receives children when His disciples would turn them away, declaring that of such is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 19:14). He values a single lost sheep enough to leave the ninety and nine to seek it (Luke 15:4-7). Each of these episodes enacts, rather than merely states, the doctrine that every human life carries a worth that does not depend on status, usefulness, or moral performance.

Jesus also corrects distortions of the created order that had crept into the religious teaching of His day. When His disciples were criticized for plucking grain on the Sabbath, He answered with a principle that reorders the relationship between man and the institutions meant to serve him: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27). The Sabbath, given as a gift to dignify man with rest, had been turned by rigid tradition into a burden that degraded him; Jesus restores the original order, in which the institution serves the image-bearer, not the reverse. In a similar reordering, when religious leaders brought a woman caught in adultery before Him, seeking to condemn her under the law while ignoring their own sin, Jesus refused to let her be used as an object for their self-righteous display: "Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more" (John 8:11). Her dignity as a person made in God's image was not erased by her sin, nor was His holiness compromised by His mercy — both truths stand together, as they must throughout this doctrine.

Zacchaeus, a despised tax collector whom the crowd regarded as beneath notice, receives from Jesus not condemnation but an invitation: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house" (Luke 19:5). Jesus explains His reasoning to the murmuring crowd: "for as much as he also is a son of Abraham" (Luke 19:9) — dignity grounded in covenant identity and, beneath that, in shared humanity, not in social respectability. At the Last Supper, Jesus Himself takes the posture of a servant, girding Himself with a towel and washing His disciples' feet (John 13:4-5) — the very Author of human dignity demonstrating that true greatness is expressed not in domination but in humble service, the dominion mandate of Genesis 1:28 fulfilled not as tyranny but as self-giving love. And Jesus affirms, by His own bodily resurrection, that the physical body is not a disposable shell to be discarded but an integral part of what it means to be human — redeemed, not abandoned. The doctrine of the resurrection of the body, developed fully in the Epistles, has its foundation here: God's original design of man as a unified being of body and spirit/soul is not undone by the fall but will be gloriously restored.

### The Apostolic Witness to the Image

The book of Acts records Paul's address to the philosophers of Athens, where he grounds a doctrine of common humanity directly in the doctrine of creation: "And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth... For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring" (Acts 17:26, 28). Paul uses this shared origin — all humanity descended from one man, all humanity made by one Creator — to confront the idolatry of Athens, arguing that it is unfitting for beings made in God's image to reduce the Godhead to gold, silver, or stone shaped by human art and device (Acts 17:29).

This doctrine of common humanity is not a New Testament innovation but a development of the table of nations recorded in Genesis 10, which traces every people group descending from Noah's sons, and of Malachi's rhetorical question to a divided covenant community: "Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother?" (Malachi 2:10). The prophet grounds the demand for covenant faithfulness between brothers in the shared fact of one Creator and one created humanity — ethnic or tribal division was never intended by God to override the deeper unity of a common origin and a common Maker. Paul's speech at Athens simply makes explicit, for a Gentile audience, what the Old Testament had already established for Israel.

Paul's epistles continue to develop the doctrine explicitly. He calls man "the image and glory of God" in 1 Corinthians 11:7, and he speaks of the believer being renewed "in knowledge after the image of him that created him" in Colossians 3:10, and further describes the "new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness" in Ephesians 4:24. These texts show that redemption does not discard the doctrine of the image of God but restores and renews it — salvation is, among other things, the reconstitution of what sin has marred in the image-bearer.

James, writing to a scattered and suffering church, appeals to this same doctrine as a check on sinful speech: "Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God" (James 3:9). The inconsistency James exposes only makes sense if every human being — including those we are tempted to curse — genuinely bears God's likeness. This is a critical New Testament development: the doctrine of the image of God is not merely theoretical but is applied directly to how believers must treat one another and, by clear extension, every person they encounter.

Paul also develops the doctrine of man's unified constitution in his teaching on the body. Against any impulse to treat the physical body as spiritually unimportant, he insists, "know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you... therefore glorify God in your body" (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). He extends this into a rich picture of human diversity held together in unity, comparing the church to a body with many members — eye, ear, hand, foot — each different, each necessary, none dispensable (1 Corinthians 12:14-22). This image, though applied to the church, rests on an anthropology that values difference without ranking human worth by function: "those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary" (1 Corinthians 12:22). Paul also commends the mind of Christ as the pattern for human relationship — not self-assertion but self-giving humility, "who, being in the form of God... made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:6-7) — true human dignity expressed, paradoxically, in voluntary lowliness rather than self-exaltation.

### Federal Headship: Adam as a Type of the One to Come

Anthropology's doctrine of man reaches a decisive turn when Paul identifies Adam not merely as the first human individual but as a federal head — one man whose action is reckoned to belong, in some real sense, to the whole race descended from him. Paul states this directly: "Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come" (Romans 5:14). Adam is here called a "figure," or type, of Christ — not because Adam resembled Christ in character, but because the structure of Adam's headship over humanity foreshadows the structure of Christ's headship over His redeemed people. As one man's act determined the condition of all who descend from him by nature, so one Man's act would determine the condition of all who are united to Him by faith (Romans 5:18-19; 1 Corinthians 15:22).

This doctrine of federal headship is what allows Anthropology, Hamartiology, and Soteriology to be told as a single coherent story rather than three disconnected topics. Man is not merely an individual studied in isolation; every human being belongs, by natural descent, to a race with a covenant head, and Scripture's good news is precisely that a new headship has been established, available to anyone who will trust the second Man rather than remain solely identified with the first. The doctrine of man, rightly understood, therefore always asks a further question of every reader: in which Adam does he presently stand? This question carries the doctrine of Anthropology directly into the doctrine that follows.

### Renewed Humanity and the Consummation

The doctrine of man reaches its fullest expression not in the original creation but in the new creation inaugurated by Christ. Paul describes the believer as a "new creature" in 2 Corinthians 5:17 — old things passed away, all things becoming new. This is not the abolition of humanity but its renewal, the reconstitution of the image of God that sin had defaced. Paul develops this renewal further in his teaching on the resurrection body, contrasting what is sown in death with what will be raised: "It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power" (1 Corinthians 15:42-43). The body itself — not merely the soul — is included in the scope of redemption; man's dual nature, established in Genesis 2:7, is honored to the very end, both halves of his being gloriously restored rather than one discarded.

Revelation closes the canon with a vision of glorified humanity: a great multitude of every nation, tribe, people, and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed and complete (Revelation 7:9-10), and finally dwelling with God in a renewed creation where former things — death, sorrow, crying, pain — have passed away (Revelation 21:3-4). The doctrine that began with man formed from the dust and given dominion in a garden ends with redeemed humanity glorified and reigning with Christ forever (Revelation 22:5).

days.title: Doctrine 4, Day 3: Christ Revealed
days.content:
Christ Revealed Jesus Christ is the true Image of the invisible God (2 Corinthians 4:4; Colossians 1:15), "the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person" (Hebrews 1:3). Where the first man, made in God's image, distorted that image through sin, Christ perfectly displays what man was always meant to be. Paul calls Him the "last Adam" and the "second man" (1 Corinthians 15:45, 47) — the one who succeeds precisely where the first Adam failed, obeying the Father completely, resisting every temptation, and living the fully human life exactly as God intended. Christ is therefore not merely humanity's Savior from outside the human race; He is humanity perfected from within it, "the firstborn among many brethren" (Romans 8:29) into whose image believers are being conformed.

This is a striking claim: to see Jesus rightly is to see what true, undistorted humanity looks like. His compassion, His obedience, His truthfulness, His dominion over creation exercised in humility rather than tyranny — all of this is the image of God, finally, fully displayed in a human life. Anthropology, then, is not complete until it arrives at Christ; He alone shows what man was made to be.

This truth also carries a promise for every believer. Scripture does not merely present Christ as a distant model to admire from afar; it promises that those who belong to Him are, even now, being transformed into that same likeness. "But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord" (2 Corinthians 3:18). The doctrine of Anthropology, rightly understood, is therefore not static — it describes not only what man was made to be at creation but what every believer in Christ is presently becoming.

This also explains why the Gospels devote such careful attention to Christ's full and genuine humanity, not merely His deity. He grew "in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man" (Luke 2:52); He hungered (Matthew 4:2), wept (John 11:35), grew weary (John 4:6), and was, in every respect, "tempted like as we are, yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15). A Christ who was only apparently human, or human in name only, could neither serve as the pattern for true humanity nor as a fitting substitute for human sin. His full humanity is not a theological technicality; it is essential to His qualification as both the last Adam and the sinless Savior this chapter's doctrines require.

days.title: Doctrine 4, Day 4: Kingdom Implications
days.content:
The doctrine of man as image-bearer has direct bearing on the Kingdom of God. If man was created to exercise dominion under God's authority, then the Kingdom is, in one sense, the restoration of that original design — humanity ruling creation rightly, under the true King, rather than in autonomous rebellion. The church, as the community of the redeemed, becomes the present demonstration of what humanity under God's reign looks like: image-bearers being renewed after the likeness of their Creator (Colossians 3:10), no longer divided by the hierarchies sin has produced — "there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28).

This has weighty implications for how the Kingdom community treats every person. Because human dignity rests on the image of God rather than on usefulness, ability, or social standing, the Kingdom community is called to honor the unborn, the elderly, the disabled, the poor, and the stranger with the same seriousness it honors the strong, the gifted, and the influential. A Kingdom shaped by this doctrine cannot tolerate the exploitation, dehumanization, or disposal of any image-bearer, for to despise a human being made in God's likeness is, in a real sense, to despise the One whose likeness he bears.

Jesus makes this connection explicit in His teaching on the final judgment, identifying Himself with "the least of these" — the hungry, the stranger, the naked, the sick, the imprisoned — such that how His people treat the vulnerable image-bearers around them is treated as how they have treated Him (Matthew 25:35-40). This is a striking Kingdom principle: dominion under God, rightly exercised, expresses itself in mercy toward the weak, not in indifference to them. And the destiny of redeemed humanity within the Kingdom is not passive but active — believers are promised a share in Christ's own reign, restoring at last the dominion mandate given in Eden: "he that overcometh... to him will I grant to sit with me in my throne" (Revelation 3:21), and "they shall reign with him a thousand years" (Revelation 20:6). The dominion lost through sin in Genesis 3 is fully recovered, not by human striving, but by grace, in Christ.

This doctrine also grounds the Kingdom ethic of neighbor-love in a way no other foundation can. When a lawyer asked Jesus to define "neighbour," Jesus answered with the parable of the Good Samaritan — a man from a despised people who stops to help a stranger left for dead, while religious insiders pass by on the other side (Luke 10:30-37). The parable does not appeal to shared nationality, shared religion, or shared social standing as the basis for neighborly love; it appeals only to shared humanity, encountered as a fellow image-bearer in need. Kingdom ethics, rightly grounded in Anthropology, know no boundary of tribe, nation, or social respectability when a fellow human being's dignity and need are at stake.

This doctrine also shapes the Kingdom's vision of human labor and vocation. Because the dominion mandate given in Eden is not revoked by the Fall but is, in Christ, being restored and redirected toward the King's purposes, ordinary work — whether in the home, the field, the marketplace, or the church — becomes a legitimate arena of Kingdom service rather than a merely secular necessity endured until worship resumes. Paul instructs believers to labor "as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Colossians 3:23), and to expect a reward from the Lord for work done in His name, regardless of whether that work is recognized or rewarded by human authorities (Colossians 3:24). The believer who plants a field, raises a family, teaches a class, or builds a house under the Lordship of Christ is, in a real sense, exercising the very dominion mandate given at creation, now recovered and redirected toward the advance of a Kingdom that will have no end.

days.title: Doctrine 4, Day 5: Practical Implications
days.content:
Living This Out Treat every person you encounter — regardless of ability, appearance, age, or usefulness to you — as a bearer of God's image, worthy of dignity and respect (James 3:9). Steward your body as God's handiwork rather than either idolizing it or neglecting it; it was formed by God and is intended for His glory (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Resist cultural pressures — in either direction — to define human worth by productivity, appearance, intelligence, or social status rather than by the image of God. Honor marriage and family according to the created order Jesus affirmed from Genesis, recognizing the one-flesh union as God's design, not a negotiable human custom (Matthew 19:4-6). Defend the sanctity of human life at every stage — the unborn, the elderly, the disabled, the dying — because every stage of human life bears God's image equally. Exercise whatever dominion or influence God has entrusted to you — in work, in creation-care, in leadership — as a steward accountable to God, not as an autonomous owner. Teach children within the covenant community to know their identity as image-bearers before they learn to measure themselves by the world's competing standards of worth (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). Practice hospitality and generosity toward the stranger and the poor, remembering that Scripture grounds the ethic of neighbor-love in shared humanity rather than shared background (Luke 10:30-37). Cultivate the capacities of reason, language, and creative work as a genuine expression of bearing God's image, offering the fruit of that labor back to Him (Genesis 2:19-20; Ephesians 4:28).

These are not abstract principles but daily postures. A believer who has internalized the doctrine of the image of God will find it shaping ordinary decisions — how to speak of a difficult coworker, how to regard an unborn child, how to treat an aging parent, how to steward a body that belongs, ultimately, to its Maker.

This doctrine should also shape the church's posture toward those the surrounding culture is tempted to dismiss — the elderly whose usefulness has passed by worldly measures, the disabled whose contribution cannot be calculated in economic terms, the unborn who cannot yet speak for themselves, and the poor who possess no social capital to offer in return. A community that has truly grasped Anthropology will be marked by a hospitality toward the weak that the watching world finds strange — not because such believers are naive about human sinfulness, addressed fully in the next doctrine, but because they have first grasped human dignity, and refuse to let sin have the last word on what a person is worth.

This doctrine also has direct bearing on how believers raise the next generation and structure family life. Because children are a heritage from the Lord and not merely a private accomplishment or an optional preference, believers are called to receive them as a genuine blessing and to take seriously the charge to raise them in the training and admonition of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4), teaching them from the earliest years that their worth rests in being made by God, not in what they achieve or how they compare to others.

Finally, this doctrine calls believers to remember whose figure they presently bear. Since every person descends from Adam and inherits his fallen condition, and since Christ stands ready to be received as the new Head of a redeemed humanity, no believer can regard Anthropology as settled business once dignity has been affirmed. The doctrine presses further, asking each reader to consider which Adam defines him, and to find, in Christ, the only Head whose life truly restores what the first Adam's headship lost.

days.title: Doctrine 4, Day 6: Summary
days.content: Summary Man and woman were created directly by God, in His image and likeness, given a unified nature of body and spirit/soul, and entrusted with dominion over the rest of creation. This dignity is not earned by human achievement; it is bestowed by divine decree and remains, even after the fall, the basis for the sanctity of every human life (Genesis 9:6). Christ, the true Image of God and the last Adam, perfectly displays what humanity was always meant to be, and believers are being renewed, day by day, into that same image. This doctrine is the necessary foundation for the two doctrines that follow. Sin can only be understood as tragedy — the corruption of something inherently good and dignified — because Anthropology first establishes what was corrupted. And salvation can only be understood as restoration because Anthropology first establishes what is being restored. The doctrine of man as image-bearer is where the whole chapter, and much of the whole gospel, begins.

doctrines.title: Hamartiology
doctrines.summary: Sin entered through one man, and death by sin; all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.

days.title: Doctrine 5, Day 1: Overview & Biblical Foundation
days.content:
Hamartiology is the biblical doctrine of sin — its origin, its nature, its universal reach, and its consequences. Having established in Anthropology the dignity with which man was created, Scripture does not allow that dignity to obscure the reality of what happened to it. Something went wrong, catastrophically and comprehensively wrong, and Scripture names it plainly: sin. This doctrine refuses two common evasions. It refuses to treat sin merely as dysfunction, mistake, or the product of poor environment and upbringing, as though man simply needs better information or better circumstances. And it refuses to treat sin as a minor blemish on an otherwise intact human goodness. Scripture presents sin as rebellion against a holy God, entering the human race through the willful disobedience of one man, with consequences reaching every one of his descendants.

The doctrine rests on this claim: sin entered the human race through the willful disobedience of Adam in the Garden of Eden, bringing spiritual death, a corrupted and sinful nature inherited by all his descendants, and subjection to physical death and futility for creation itself. Sin is rebellion against God's revealed character and law — not merely poor choices, social dysfunction, or unfortunate circumstance. Every human being, without exception, is born in sin and sins personally, and stands in need of a Savior; no one can remedy this condition by self-effort, religious performance, or good works.

## Biblical Foundation

The controlling text for the origin of sin is Genesis 3, the record of the Fall. Tempted by the serpent to doubt God's word and God's goodness, Eve took of the forbidden fruit and ate, and gave also unto her husband, and he did eat (Genesis 3:6). This single act of willful disobedience — not ignorance, not accident, but a deliberate choice to disbelieve and disobey God's clear command — is the entrance point of sin into the human race. The consequences follow immediately: the eyes of both were opened, they knew they were naked, they hid from the presence of the Lord, and God pronounced judgment on the serpent, the woman, the man, and the ground itself (Genesis 3:7-19), culminating in their expulsion from the garden and from access to the tree of life (Genesis 3:22-24).

Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned. Romans 5:12

Romans 5:12 provides the theological explanation of what Genesis 3 narrates: "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned" (Romans 5:12). This text establishes that Adam's sin was not merely his own private failure but the doorway through which sin and death entered the entire human race — every descendant of Adam inherits both the guilt and the corrupted nature that flow from his fall.

Romans 3:23 states the universal scope of sin's reach with unqualified plainness: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). No exception is made for any class, nation, or individual — Jew and Gentile alike, the text has just argued (Romans 3:9), are all under sin. And Romans 6:23 states sin's wage with equal plainness: "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Romans 6:23). This verse establishes both the just consequence of sin — death, in its fullest sense, physical and spiritual and eternal — and, in the same breath, points forward to the doctrine of Soteriology that answers it.

A fourth foundational text confirms that no human exception exists to this universal condition. Solomon states it as settled wisdom: "For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not" (Ecclesiastes 7:20), and at the dedication of the temple he prays with the same assumption: "if they sin against thee (for there is no man that sinneth not)" (1 Kings 8:46). Isaiah adds the sharpest possible image for the futility of human righteousness apart from grace: "all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags" (Isaiah 64:6). These texts, spanning the wisdom and prophetic literature, close off any appeal to human exception. Whatever partial goodness may be observed in human conduct, Scripture will not allow it to be mistaken for the righteousness God's holiness requires.

The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? Jeremiah 17:9
