days.title: Doctrine 5, Day 2: Biblical Development
days.content:
### The Fall and Its Spread in the Law

Genesis 3 stands as the hinge of the entire biblical narrative. Before it, creation is repeatedly pronounced good, very good (Genesis 1:31). After it, the text moves swiftly to catalogue sin's spread: Cain's jealous murder of his brother Abel (Genesis 4:8), Lamech's boastful violence (Genesis 4:23-24), and finally a generation so corrupted that "every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5), provoking the judgment of the flood. Even after the flood, sin persists undiminished — Noah's own drunkenness and his family's dysfunction (Genesis 9:20-25), and the proud rebellion of Babel, where humanity united not to glorify God but to make a name for itself (Genesis 11:4).

### Sin's Shame and God's Provision of Covering

The immediate response of Adam and Eve to their own sin is deeply instructive for the doctrine. Their eyes opened, they perceive their nakedness for the first time as a cause for shame, and their own remedy is entirely inadequate: "they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons" (Genesis 3:7) — a self-made covering, born of shame, that cannot withstand God's presence and does not survive their attempt to hide from Him (Genesis 3:8-10). What man's own effort could not accomplish, God Himself provides: "Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them" (Genesis 3:21). This single verse carries immense theological weight — it requires the death of an animal, the first recorded death in Scripture, to provide a covering adequate for sinful man to stand, however imperfectly, before a holy God. The pattern set here — human effort at self-covering proving insufficient, substitutionary death providing what man could not provide for himself — becomes the template for the entire sacrificial system that follows and, ultimately, for the finished work of Christ, who alone provides a covering for sin that will never wear out or prove insufficient (Romans 13:14; Galatians 3:27).

The remainder of the Pentateuch continues to develop this doctrine through the giving of the Law. The Law does not create sin; it exposes and defines it. Paul later explains this function directly: "for by the law is the knowledge of sin" (Romans 3:20), and "I had not known sin, but by the law" (Romans 7:7). The sacrificial system instituted in Leviticus — the sin offering, the trespass offering, the Day of Atonement — presupposes and dramatizes the seriousness of sin at every turn: it cannot simply be overlooked or excused; it requires a substitute, atoning blood, to be dealt with rightly before a holy God (Leviticus 17:11). The repeated, unending cycle of animal sacrifice testifies both to sin's constant recurrence in the life of God's own covenant people and to the inadequacy of animal blood to finally remove it — a tension the book of Hebrews will later resolve fully in Christ (Hebrews 10:1-4).

The history of Israel that follows the giving of the Law becomes an extended demonstration of humanity's inability to escape sin's grip even under the most favorable conditions imaginable — a chosen people, a revealed law, prophets sent to warn and correct, and still, generation after generation, the same pattern of disobedience recurs. The wilderness generation, delivered by mighty miracles, still murmurs, rebels, and worships a golden calf within weeks of receiving the Law (Exodus 32:1-8). The era of the Judges repeats a grim cycle — sin, oppression, cries for deliverance, rescue, and relapse — summarized by the book's own closing verdict: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25). Even Israel's most celebrated king, chosen after God's own heart, falls into adultery and murder (2 Samuel 11), and the kingdom itself eventually divides and, over centuries, is carried into exile for its persistent unfaithfulness. This sustained historical witness confirms Paul's later verdict: "the law worketh wrath... for by the law is the knowledge of sin" (Romans 4:15; 3:20) — the Law could expose sin with perfect clarity, but it could never, in itself, cure the heart that kept producing it.

The Law also warns that sin, though sometimes hidden for a season, is never ultimately concealed from God's notice. Moses tells the tribes of Reuben and Gad plainly, "be sure your sin will find you out" (Numbers 32:23), and the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 describe in painful detail the consequences that follow a nation's persistent, unrepented rebellion against its God. This is a critical development in the doctrine: sin is not a private matter between the sinner and his own conscience. It is transgression against a covenant-keeping God who sees, who remembers, and who will hold every act of rebellion to account, whether that reckoning comes in this life or the next.

### Sin in the Writings and Prophets

Nowhere in Scripture is the internal reality of sin explored with more searching honesty than in Psalm 51, David's confession after his sin with Bathsheba. He does not minimize his guilt or attribute it to circumstance: "Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions. Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me" (Psalm 51:1-3). Strikingly, David traces his sinfulness back further than his own actions, to his very origin: "Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me" (Psalm 51:5) — a clear witness to what later theology calls original sin, the inherited corruption of nature present from conception, not merely sin as isolated acts.

### The Many Facets of Sin: Transgression, Iniquity, and Trespass

Scripture does not describe sin with a single flat term but with a cluster of related words, each capturing a distinct facet of the same reality. David's own words in Psalm 32 gather several of these facets together in deliberate parallel: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity" (Psalm 32:1-2). Transgression describes sin as a boundary crossed — a deliberate stepping over a line God has drawn. Sin, in its most general sense, describes a falling short, a failure to meet the standard God requires. Iniquity describes something more internal still — a crookedness or twistedness of the heart itself, not merely a single deviant act but a bent condition underlying it. Paul later adds the language of trespass, a false step or stumbling that leaves the sinner in debt to the one wronged (Ephesians 2:1; Matthew 6:12). Together, these overlapping terms teach that sin cannot be reduced to any single category — it is at once a boundary violated, a standard missed, a heart deformed, and a debt incurred — and any doctrine of sin that flattens this richness into a single dimension has not yet reckoned with the full biblical picture.

### God's Patience Amid Sin's Provocation

Though sin provokes God's righteous wrath, Scripture is equally emphatic that God does not deal with sinners as swiftly or as severely as their sin deserves. Paul asks the self-righteous moralist in Romans, "despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?" (Romans 2:4), and Peter explains the apparent delay of final judgment in the same terms: "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance" (2 Peter 3:9). This patience is not indifference to sin's seriousness — the wrath already described in this doctrine remains real and certain — but a merciful delay, a space granted for repentance before judgment falls. Nahum captures both truths in a single verse: "The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked" (Nahum 1:3) — patience and justice held together without contradiction, precisely as this whole doctrine of sin has held dignity and ruin, mercy and holiness, together throughout.

The prophets confront Israel's sin relentlessly, refusing to let ritual observance substitute for genuine obedience. Isaiah records the Lord's indictment: "But your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear" (Isaiah 59:2), establishing that sin's fundamental consequence is separation — a broken relationship with God, not merely a broken rule.

The prophets also expose a particular form of sin that religious people are especially prone to: substituting ritual performance for genuine obedience. Samuel confronts Saul's partial, self-justified obedience with a principle that reorders the whole relationship between ritual and righteousness: "Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams" (1 Samuel 15:22). Isaiah delivers an even sharper indictment against a nation that had multiplied its sacrifices while neglecting justice and mercy: "To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the LORD... Bring no more vain oblations... Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings" (Isaiah 1:11-16). Amos, likewise, records the Lord's rejection of feasts and offerings offered by a people indifferent to justice: "let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream" (Amos 5:21-24). This is a critical development in the doctrine: sin is not remedied by religious activity performed alongside continued disobedience; God is not deceived by outward performance that leaves the heart untouched.

Isaiah 53:6 gives the doctrine its most memorable summary: "All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all" — a verse that both states humanity's universal wandering and points directly toward the Servant who would bear that iniquity. Jeremiah diagnoses the human heart itself as the source of the problem: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" (Jeremiah 17:9) — sin is not merely behavioral but rooted in the depths of human nature, deceiving even the one who possesses it.

### Sin as an Offense Ultimately Against God

Though sin frequently harms other people, Scripture is careful to locate its deepest offense against God Himself. David's sin against Bathsheba and Uriah was, by any human accounting, a sin against them; yet in his confession, David says, "Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight" (Psalm 51:4). This is not a denial of the human harm his sin caused — Nathan's confrontation makes that harm explicit (2 Samuel 12:1-12) — but a recognition that every sin against a fellow image-bearer is, at the same time and more fundamentally, a sin against the God whose image that person bears and whose law has been broken. Joseph resists Potiphar's wife's temptation to adultery with the same logic: "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9) — his primary category for the sin she proposes is not merely betrayal of his master's trust but offense against God. This does not diminish the real horizontal harm sin causes between people; it explains why that harm is so serious in the first place — because every person wronged bears the image of the God against whom the wrong is ultimately committed.

### The Believer's Ongoing Struggle Against Sin

Hamartiology is not merely a doctrine about the unconverted; Scripture is honest that even the regenerate believer continues to wrestle with sin's presence, though no longer under its dominion. Paul's description of this struggle in Romans 7 is unusually personal and unguarded: "For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I" (Romans 7:15), concluding with a cry that only makes sense on the far side of genuine conversion: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" (Romans 7:24). Galatians describes this same ongoing tension as warfare between two opposing principles within the believer: "the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other" (Galatians 5:17). This doctrine matters pastorally: the presence of an ongoing struggle against sin in a believer's life is not, by itself, evidence of a false or failed conversion; Scripture presents it as the normal, if uncomfortable, experience of every believer this side of glorification, to be fought earnestly through the Spirit's power rather than either denied or surrendered to.

### The Universality and Depth of Sin's Corruption

Scripture describes sin not merely as a scattering of isolated bad acts but as a corruption reaching every faculty of the human person — mind, will, and affections alike. The psalmist traces this corruption to man's very origin: "The wicked are estranged from the womb: they go astray as soon as they be born, speaking lies" (Psalm 58:3), echoing David's confession in Psalm 51 that sin is present before any deliberate act is committed. Jeremiah presses the point further with a vivid picture of sin's grip: "Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil" (Jeremiah 13:23) — sin is not a removable layer over an otherwise good nature but has become, apart from grace, second nature itself.

This corruption reaches the mind as well as the will. The wisdom literature repeatedly contrasts the way that "seemeth right unto a man" with its true end, which is death (Proverbs 14:12), teaching that fallen human reasoning cannot be trusted as a reliable guide to righteousness apart from God's revealed word. Isaiah likewise confronts a generation whose moral reasoning has become inverted: "Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness" (Isaiah 5:20). Sin, in other words, does not leave the intellect untouched while corrupting only behavior; it distorts judgment itself, so that fallen man cannot be relied upon to reason his own way back to God.

### The Deceitfulness and Progression of Sin

Scripture describes sin not as a static condition but as a living process, one that deceives before it destroys. The writer of Hebrews warns believers against being "hardened through the deceitfulness of sin" (Hebrews 3:13) — sin does not usually announce itself honestly; it presents itself as pleasurable, reasonable, or harmless, and only afterward reveals its true cost. James traces this progression with precision: "every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death" (James 1:14-15). The image is deliberately biological — temptation conceives, sin is born, and sin, left to mature, brings forth death as its natural offspring. This progression explains why Scripture consistently calls for sin to be dealt with early and decisively, at the level of desire, rather than tolerated until it has fully matured into open, destructive action.

### Sin and Death: A Three-fold Consequence

God's warning to Adam in the garden was direct: "in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die" (Genesis 2:17). Adam did not fall dead physically the moment he ate the forbidden fruit, yet Scripture treats the warning as having been fulfilled immediately and continues to unfold its full meaning across the rest of the canon. Death, in biblical usage, is not a single event but a three-fold reality. Spiritual death is immediate — the fellowship with God that Adam and Eve had known was instantly ruptured, and they hid from His presence (Genesis 3:8); Paul describes every unconverted person as, in this same sense, "dead in trespasses and sins" (Ephesians 2:1), spiritually lifeless toward God even while physically alive. Physical death follows in time — "dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Genesis 3:19), the sentence every subsequent generation inherits, "for that all have sinned" (Romans 5:12). And eternal death, the final and most terrible sense of the word, awaits those who die without having been reconciled to God through Christ — described as "the second death" and "the lake of fire" (Revelation 20:14). Sin's wage, in other words, is not a single loss but a comprehensive one, touching every dimension of human existence — present fellowship with God, bodily life, and eternal destiny alike — which is precisely why the salvation Christ offers must be, and is, comprehensive as well.

### Sin's Effect on Creation Itself

The consequences of the Fall are not confined to the human race alone. When God pronounces judgment on Adam, the ground itself is included in the curse: "cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life; thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee" (Genesis 3:17-18). Man's rebellion did not merely damage his relationship with God; it introduced disorder into the created order he was appointed to steward. Paul develops this cosmic dimension of sin's effect in Romans 8, describing creation itself as subjected to "vanity" and "the bondage of corruption," groaning and travailing in pain, awaiting a liberation that will come only when the sons of God are finally revealed in glory (Romans 8:19-22). Sin's ruin, in other words, reaches beyond the individual sinner into the fabric of the created world — a truth that anticipates the full restoration described in Doctrine 7, the Theology of Creation.

### Common Grace Amid Universal Sin

Total depravity, rightly understood, does not mean that every sinner is as fully wicked in outward practice as he could possibly be, nor that no good act of any kind can be observed among unbelievers. Scripture teaches that God, in His kindness, restrains sin's full expression in the world and continues to show a measure of undeserved goodness even to those in open rebellion against Him. Jesus teaches that the Father "maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust" (Matthew 5:45), and Paul tells the pagan crowd at Lystra that God "left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness" (Acts 14:17). This common grace explains why unregenerate people are capable of real kindness, real civic order, real artistic and intellectual achievement — such capacities are not evidence against the doctrine of universal depravity, but evidence of a restraining, sustaining kindness God extends even to a fallen world, withholding, for a time, the full and immediate consequences sin deserves, and granting space for the gospel to be preached and received (2 Peter 3:9).

### The Scope of Sin: Commission and Omission

Scripture defines sin broadly enough to include not only wrongful acts committed but also right acts neglected. James states this dimension of the doctrine directly: "Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin" (James 4:17). This closes off a common evasion — the assumption that avoiding overt wrongdoing is sufficient righteousness before God. The parable of the sheep and the goats presses the same point: those condemned are condemned not for violent crimes but for failing to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, and visit the sick and imprisoned (Matthew 25:41-45) — sins of omission, neglect of the good that was known and possible but left undone. Hamartiology, rightly taught, therefore examines a life's failures to love and serve, not merely its list of overt transgressions.

### Sin and the Conscience

Even where God's written law has not been received, Scripture teaches that sin's reality is confirmed by the testimony of conscience within every human heart. Paul writes of the Gentiles, "which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another" (Romans 2:15). This internal witness explains why guilt and shame are universal human experiences, present even among peoples who have never heard the biblical revelation of sin — the conscience itself testifies to a moral order its bearer has violated. Paul warns elsewhere that this conscience, if repeatedly resisted, can become "seared with a hot iron" (1 Timothy 4:2), progressively less sensitive to sin's true seriousness — a sober warning that the moral compass built into every image-bearer is not indestructible, and its testimony can be deadened, though never entirely silenced, by persistent rebellion.

### Sin Pictured as Slavery: Bondage and the Need for a Liberator

Scripture frequently pictures sin not merely as a series of discrete acts but as a master to whom the sinner is enslaved, unable to break free by his own resolve. Jesus states the principle directly: "Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin" (John 8:34) — the very structure of repeated sin creates a bondage the sinner did not fully anticipate when he first indulged it. Paul develops the same picture at length in Romans, describing the unconverted as those who once yielded their members "servants to uncleanness and to iniquity unto iniquity" (Romans 6:19), and reminding the Ephesians that they were, before Christ, "children of disobedience," following "the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience" (Ephesians 2:2). Paul elsewhere catalogues his own pre-conversion condition among a litany of similar bondages: "we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures" (Titus 3:3).

This imagery of bondage matters for the doctrine of sin because it explains why sin cannot be broken by willpower or resolution alone, however sincere. A slave does not free himself by trying harder to be a better slave; he requires a liberator with the authority and power to break the chains from outside his own captivity. This is precisely what the doctrine of sin, read honestly, prepares the reader to expect — and precisely what the doctrine of salvation, treated next in this chapter, supplies. Jesus states the resolution in the same breath as the diagnosis: "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed" (John 8:36).

### Sin's Root: Idolatry

Scripture repeatedly traces the many branches of sin back to a single root: the displacement of God from His rightful place at the center of human worship and allegiance. The first and second commandments forbid this displacement directly — "Thou shalt have no other gods before me... Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image" (Exodus 20:3-4) — establishing idolatry as the fountainhead sin from which every other transgression flows. Paul makes this connection explicit in Romans 1, describing humanity's fundamental sin as exchanging "the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man" (Romans 1:23) and, more broadly, worshiping and serving "the creature more than the Creator" (Romans 1:25) — and it is precisely this exchange that gives rise to the catalogue of moral corruption that follows in the rest of the chapter. Sin, at its root, is not merely the breaking of isolated rules but the dethroning of God in the heart and the enthronement of something else — self, pleasure, possessions, power, or another person — in His place. Paul names covetousness itself as a species of idolatry (Colossians 3:5), showing how ordinary, everyday sins trace back to this same fundamental misplacement of worship.

### Spiritual Blindness and the Need for Illumination

Sin's corruption extends to the sinner's very capacity to perceive spiritual truth clearly. Paul describes unbelievers as those "in whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ... should shine unto them" (2 Corinthians 4:4), and elsewhere as having "the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart" (Ephesians 4:18). Jesus' healing of the man born blind in John 9 becomes, in His own hands, a living parable of this deeper spiritual condition — the Pharisees, who could physically see perfectly well, are the ones Jesus pronounces genuinely blind: "If ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth" (John 9:41). This blindness is a critical link between the doctrines of this chapter: sin does not merely corrupt behavior; it disables the very faculty by which a sinner might otherwise recognize his need and turn toward the remedy. This is precisely why Soteriology, treated next, must involve more than the presentation of true information — it requires a sovereign, gracious work of illumination, opening blind eyes that could never open themselves (2 Corinthians 4:6).

### Sin's Corporate and Generational Reach

Sin in Scripture is never merely a private matter contained within the individual sinner. The Law warns that the effects of persistent sin can extend across generations within a family or nation: God describes Himself as one "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me" (Exodus 20:5) — not a transfer of individual guilt, since Ezekiel 18:20 makes clear that each soul bears its own guilt, but a sober warning that sin's patterns and consequences ripple outward, shaping households and communities long after the initial act. The account of Achan in Joshua 7 shows sin's corporate dimension vividly: one man's secret disobedience brings defeat and judgment upon the whole camp of Israel, "for they also have transgressed my covenant" (Joshua 7:11), until the sin is exposed and dealt with. Sin, in other words, is never merely private; it has social, relational, and communal consequences that Scripture refuses to minimize.

### Sin Among the Nations: Universal Guilt Beyond Israel

The prophets do not confine the diagnosis of sin to God's covenant people alone. Amos opens his prophecy with a sweeping indictment of the surrounding nations — Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab — each pronounced guilty and marked for judgment "for three transgressions... and for four" before the prophet ever turns his indictment toward Judah and Israel themselves (Amos 1:3-2:8). None of these nations had received the law given at Sinai, yet each is held accountable for cruelty, treachery, and violence against fellow human beings — a clear witness that moral accountability before God does not depend on possessing the written law, a principle Paul later states explicitly of the Gentiles, who "shew the work of the law written in their hearts" (Romans 2:14-15). Isaiah and Jeremiah likewise pronounce oracles of judgment against Babylon, Egypt, Moab, and the nations round about (Isaiah 13-23; Jeremiah 46-51), confirming that sin's reach and God's just response to it are never limited to the visible covenant community. This canonical witness anticipates Paul's later verdict that the whole world, Jew and Gentile without distinction, stands guilty before God (Romans 3:19) — a truth already sounded centuries earlier in the oracles of the prophets against nations that never received Moses' law.

### Presumptuous Sin and Sins of Ignorance

The Law distinguishes, without softening the seriousness of either, between sins committed unwittingly and sins committed with a high hand. Provision is made under the sacrificial system for sin committed in ignorance — "if a soul sin, and commit any of these things which are forbidden to be done by the commandments of the LORD... though he wist it not, yet is he guilty" (Leviticus 5:17) — such sin still requires atonement, but the text distinguishes it from sin committed knowingly and defiantly: "the soul that doeth ought presumptuously... the same reproacheth the LORD; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people" (Numbers 15:30). David, aware of the danger of sins he cannot even perceive in himself, prays, "Who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults. Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me" (Psalm 19:12-13). This distinction matters for a full doctrine of sin: culpability is real even where awareness is incomplete, since the standard is God's holiness rather than human self-perception, yet Scripture treats willful, defiant sin — sin committed with full knowledge and in open contempt of God's command — as carrying a particular gravity, a distinction the writer of Hebrews later presses with equal seriousness concerning willful sin against the greater light of the gospel (Hebrews 10:26-27).

### Sin's Universal Reach Confirmed by Scripture's Greatest Saints

Romans 3:23's claim that "all have sinned" is not merely a doctrinal assertion but a verdict confirmed repeatedly by Scripture's own honest narration of its most commended figures. Noah, described as "a just man and perfect in his generations" who "walked with God" (Genesis 6:9), is shown only a few chapters later lying drunk and exposed in his tent (Genesis 9:21). Abraham, called the father of the faithful and the friend of God (James 2:23), twice deceives foreign kings about his relationship to Sarah out of self-protective fear (Genesis 12:11-13; 20:2). Moses, who spoke with God face to face as a man speaks with his friend (Exodus 33:11), was barred from entering the Promised Land for striking the rock in anger rather than speaking to it as God commanded (Numbers 20:10-12). David, a man after God's own heart (1 Samuel 13:14), committed adultery and arranged a murder to conceal it (2 Samuel 11). Scripture does not conceal or excuse the failures of its heroes; it records them with unflinching honesty, precisely because its purpose is never to present flawless human examples but to demonstrate, even through its most faithful figures, that no one — however greatly used by God — stands outside the reach of this doctrine.

### Christ's Confrontation of Sin in the Gospels

Jesus intensifies rather than relaxes the Old Testament's diagnosis of sin. In the Sermon on the Mount, He locates sin's true origin not merely in outward acts but in the heart's inward disposition: anger is akin to murder (Matthew 5:21-22), lust is akin to adultery (Matthew 5:27-28). Later He states the principle directly: "For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, covetousness, wickedness, deceit, lasciviousness, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness: all these evil things come from within, and defile the man" (Mark 7:21-23). This is a crucial development in the doctrine: sin is not primarily an external violation to be managed by external rules, but an internal corruption that produces external acts — the very corruption of nature David confessed in Psalm 51 and that Genesis 3 introduced into the race.

Yet Jesus does not merely diagnose sin; He confronts it directly in the lives of those He encounters, calling sinners to repentance rather than despair. "I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance" (Luke 5:32), He declares, and His ministry is characterized by table fellowship with tax collectors and sinners that scandalized the religious establishment of His day (Luke 15:1-2). This pattern reveals something essential to the doctrine: sin is universal — even the most scrupulously religious harbor it, as Jesus exposes repeatedly in His confrontations with the Pharisees (Matthew 23) — and yet sin is not beyond the reach of divine mercy. Jesus' entire earthly mission moves inexorably toward the cross, where He will deal with sin not merely by diagnosing it but by bearing it.

Jesus' parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector exposes the particular danger of religious self-righteousness as a cover for sin. The Pharisee, thanking God that he is "not as other men are," stands in sharp contrast to the tax collector, who "would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner." Jesus' verdict overturns every expectation: "this man went down to his house justified rather than the other" (Luke 18:9-14). The rich young ruler receives a similar exposure — confident in his own law-keeping, he departs sorrowful when Jesus reveals the idolatry beneath his outward obedience (Mark 10:17-22). And when Jesus approaches Jerusalem, He does not merely observe the city's sin from a distance but weeps over it: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem... how often would I have gathered thy children together... and ye would not!" (Matthew 23:37). Sin, in the Gospels, is confronted not with detached analysis but with the grief of a Savior who came to save exactly the sinners His diagnosis exposes.

### The Apostolic Doctrine of Sin

Paul's letter to the Romans gives the most systematic New Testament treatment of Hamartiology. Romans 1 traces humanity's sin to its root: a refusal to glorify God as God and give Him thanks, resulting in futile thinking, darkened hearts, and idolatry (Romans 1:21-23), which in turn gives rise to every form of moral corruption catalogued in the chapter's closing verses (Romans 1:24-32). Romans 2 extends the indictment to those who judge others while practicing the same sins themselves (Romans 2:1). Romans 3 concludes the argument with an unanswerable verdict, quoting extensively from the Psalms and Isaiah: "There is none righteous, no, not one... for all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:10, 23). Romans 5 then explains the mechanism by which this universal condition came to be: through Adam's one act of disobedience, sin and death entered and spread to all, so that "by one man's disobedience many were made sinners" (Romans 5:19).

Ephesians 2 describes the pre-conversion condition of every believer in the starkest terms available in Scripture: "dead in trespasses and sins... children of wrath, even as others" (Ephesians 2:1-3). This is not a description of sinners as merely sick, weakened, or handicapped, but as spiritually dead — utterly unable, apart from God's intervening grace, to move toward God on their own initiative. James adds that sin, when conceived, "bringeth forth death" (James 1:15), tracing the full life-cycle of temptation to sin to death. And John, writing to believers who might be tempted toward spiritual pride, insists: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us... If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us" (1 John 1:8, 10) — even believers must continually acknowledge and confess ongoing sin, though they are no longer enslaved to it as they once were.

Paul catalogues the specific expressions of sin's corruption with unusual particularity in his letter to the Galatians, listing "the works of the flesh" — adultery, fornication, uncleanness, idolatry, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, envyings, murders, drunkenness, and more — warning that "they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God" (Galatians 5:19-21). James traces the social devastation sin produces to its root in the human heart: "From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?" (James 4:1) — the conflicts between people are, at bottom, the overflow of sin within people. Paul also names sin's relational effect in its starkest terms: sinners are, apart from Christ, "enemies" of God, requiring not mere improvement but reconciliation (Romans 5:10) — a hostility that no amount of self-effort can resolve, since the hostility is toward God Himself, not merely toward His commands.

### The Wrath of God Against Sin

Scripture does not present God's response to sin as mere disappointment but as holy, righteous wrath — the necessary response of a perfectly just God to willful rebellion against Him. Paul opens his argument in Romans with this very truth: "For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men" (Romans 1:18). John states with equal bluntness, "He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him" (John 3:36) — wrath is not merely a future possibility for the unrepentant but a present reality already resting upon those outside of Christ. Paul warns believers not to be deceived by those who would excuse sin, "for because of these things cometh the wrath of God upon the children of disobedience" (Ephesians 5:6). This doctrine is essential to a right understanding of sin — if God's holiness did not require a just response to sin, sin could hardly be called serious at all, and the cross, where that wrath was fully satisfied, would lose its meaning entirely.

### Sin's Final Reckoning in Revelation

The canon closes with sin's ultimate and final reckoning. Revelation 20 records the great white throne judgment, where the dead, small and great, stand before God, and the books are opened, and the dead are judged according to their works (Revelation 20:11-13). Those whose names are not found written in the book of life are cast into the lake of fire, described as the second death (Revelation 20:14-15). This is not vindictiveness but the necessary conclusion of a holy God's just response to unrepented rebellion. Yet Revelation does not end there — it ends with a new heaven and a new earth in which sin, death, sorrow, and pain have no more place (Revelation 21:4), the final and complete undoing of everything Genesis 3 set in motion, accomplished entirely through the Lamb who was slain.

days.title: Doctrine 5, Day 3: Christ Revealed
days.content:
Christ Revealed The doctrine of sin exists in Scripture to prepare the reader for the necessity of Christ. If sin were a minor flaw, a Savior who died would be an overreaction; if sin is what Scripture says it is — rebellion against a holy God, corrupting the whole person, meriting death — then only a sinless substitute could deal with it rightly. Scripture presents Christ as exactly that: "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him" (2 Corinthians 5:21). He "did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth" (1 Peter 2:22), and was tempted in every way as we are, "yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15). "Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree" (1 Peter 2:24) — Christ did not merely diagnose humanity's sin from a distance; He carried its full weight and penalty in Himself.

This is the decisive difference between Christ's confrontation of sin and every other approach offered by human religion or philosophy. He does not merely instruct sinners how to do better; He bears, personally and completely, the penalty their sin deserved, satisfying the justice of God so that mercy can be extended without compromising His holiness.

Christ's sinlessness is not incidental to His mission but essential to it. Under the sacrificial pattern established in the Law, only an unblemished offering could be presented to God (Leviticus 22:19-21); Christ is that offering — "a lamb without blemish and without spot" (1 Peter 1:19). Had He carried any sin of His own, His death could have paid, at most, His own debt. Because He carried none, His death is able to pay the debt of others. Hebrews draws out the full weight of this: "such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners... who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself" (Hebrews 7:26-27). Sin's doctrine, taken seriously, makes the sinlessness of Christ not a minor biographical detail but the very hinge on which the sinner's rescue turns.

Christ's confrontation of sin at the cross also displays something Hamartiology alone could never fully anticipate: that God's holiness and God's love meet, without compromise to either, in a single act. Paul states this directly: God set forth Christ "to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins... that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus" (Romans 3:25-26). The cross does not resolve the tension between God's holiness and His mercy by softening one or the other; it satisfies both fully, at once, in the person of Christ. Sin is taken with total seriousness — the penalty is paid in full — and mercy is extended with total freedom — the sinner is fully forgiven. No doctrine of sin less severe than the one this chapter has presented could account for a remedy this costly; no lesser remedy could have been sufficient for a doctrine of sin this severe.

days.title: Doctrine 5, Day 4: Kingdom Implications
days.content:
Sin is, at its root, rebellion against the reign of God — a refusal of His rightful rule, a rejection of His King. Every sin, however small it may appear, is in essence the same rebellion that filled Eden: "Yea, hath God said?" (Genesis 3:1) repeated in ten thousand variations. This means the Kingdom of God cannot advance by human effort, moral reform, or improved circumstance, because sin is not merely a behavioral problem to be managed but a fundamental orientation of rebellion to be conquered. The Kingdom advances only as the King Himself deals with sin decisively — which He has, at the cross — and as His Spirit applies that victory to individual hearts through the new birth.

The church, as the community of the King's people, must therefore hold two truths together without compromise: sin is to be taken with utmost seriousness, confronted honestly, and never excused or normalized within the fellowship (1 Corinthians 5); and sin is never to be met with despair, because the King who reigns has already dealt with it fully at the cross, and forgiveness, not condemnation, defines how His people are to be received (Romans 8:1).

This doctrine also clarifies why the Kingdom cannot be advanced by mere social reform or improved circumstance, however good such efforts may be in their own place. Because sin corrupts the heart, not merely the environment, external improvement without internal transformation leaves the fundamental rebellion untouched. The Kingdom advances only as the King Himself, through His Spirit, produces the internal change no external program can achieve — the new heart and new spirit the prophets promised (Ezekiel 36:26), given not by human effort but by divine grace working from within.

This doctrine also clarifies the nature of the Kingdom's conflict with the present age. Paul describes believers as having once walked "according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air" (Ephesians 2:2), language that identifies sin not merely as isolated wrongdoing but as participation in a present spiritual order opposed to God's reign. The Kingdom's advance is therefore not merely the improvement of individual behavior but a transfer of allegiance — from darkness to light, from one master to another: "For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light" (Ephesians 5:8). Every advance of the Kingdom in a human heart is, in this sense, a small but real skirmish in a much larger conflict, the outcome of which was already decided at the cross.

days.title: Doctrine 5, Day 5: Practical Implications
days.content:
Living This Out Confess sin honestly and specifically rather than minimizing it as a mistake, a phase, or someone else's fault (1 John 1:9). Refuse to excuse sin by appeal to circumstance, upbringing, or personality — Scripture locates the problem in the heart, not merely the environment (Jeremiah 17:9). Guard the heart, not merely outward behavior, recognizing that sin begins in thought and desire before it ever becomes visible action (Mark 7:21-23). Practice ongoing repentance as a daily posture of the Christian life, not a one-time event at conversion only. Extend the same grace toward others' sin that God has extended toward yours, refusing self-righteous comparison (Matthew 7:3-5). Resist the temptation to seek self-improvement or religious performance as a substitute for genuine repentance and dependence on grace. Teach children and new believers to recognize sin's deceitfulness early, so that conscience is trained by Scripture rather than gradually seared by habitual compromise (1 Timothy 4:2). Remember that creation itself groans under sin's effects, and let that truth temper both despair over present brokenness and presumption that this world, as it is, is all there will ever be (Romans 8:19-22). Distinguish, in self-examination, between sins committed in ignorance and sins committed presumptuously, taking special care to resist known sin rather than excusing it as unavoidable weakness (Psalm 19:13). Do not measure sin's seriousness by whether it harms another person visibly, remembering that every sin is first and finally an offense against God Himself (Psalm 51:4). Watch for sin's deceitfulness in its earliest stages — at the level of desire and thought — rather than waiting until it has matured into visible, destructive action (James 1:14-15).

A believer who takes this doctrine seriously will neither despair over the depth of human sinfulness nor grow careless about its danger. Sin is taken seriously precisely because grace has already been found sufficient to answer it — the doctrine of sin makes sense, and becomes bearable to face honestly, only in light of the doctrine that follows it.

Parents and teachers within the covenant community carry a particular responsibility in light of this doctrine — to raise children and disciple believers with an honest, age-appropriate account of sin, neither so severe that grace is obscured nor so soft that sin's true danger is hidden. The same balance applies to how the church disciplines its own members: confrontation of sin within the body must be pursued not to shame but to restore, "considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted" (Galatians 6:1), always with the aim of repentance and restoration rather than mere punishment.

This doctrine also warns against the assumption that sin only matters where its consequences are dramatic or public. Scripture's witness against the nations in Amos 1-2, none of whom possessed the written law, establishes that moral accountability before God is universal, not confined to those who have received explicit revelation. Every person, believer and unbeliever alike, is answerable to the God whose law is written, in some measure, even upon hearts that never open a Bible (Romans 2:14-15) — a sober truth that should temper any tendency to regard those outside the faith as morally neutral rather than genuinely, if unknowingly, in need of the same grace the church proclaims.

days.title: Doctrine 5, Day 6: Summary
days.content: Summary Sin entered the human race through Adam's willful disobedience in the Garden, bringing spiritual death, a corrupted nature inherited by every one of his descendants, and subjection to physical death. Sin is rebellion against God's revealed character and law — not mere dysfunction or misfortune — and it reaches every human being without exception, so that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). No one can remedy this condition through self-effort, religious performance, or good works; the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). This doctrine is not the final word of this chapter, but it is the necessary word before the final one can be understood rightly. Having seen man's dignity in Anthropology and man's ruin in Hamartiology, the chapter now turns to the doctrine that answers both — Soteriology, the doctrine of salvation, in which the gift of God, eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord, is offered freely to sinners who cannot save themselves.

doctrines.title: Soteriology
doctrines.summary: By grace are ye saved through faith; salvation is God's gift from first to last.

days.title: Doctrine 6, Day 1: Overview & Biblical Foundation
days.content:
Soteriology is the doctrine of salvation — how God rescues sinners from the ruin described in Hamartiology and restores them to the dignity and purpose described in Anthropology. This doctrine is the hinge on which the entire chapter turns, and indeed on which the entire gospel turns. Having established that man was made in dignity and that man fell into comprehensive ruin through sin, Scripture does not leave the story there. It proclaims, with unwavering consistency from Genesis to Revelation, that God Himself has acted to save.

The doctrine rests on this claim: salvation is entirely by God's grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ alone — not by works, ritual, or merit. Christ's death satisfies divine justice on behalf of sinners; those who repent and believe are regenerated (born again), justified (declared righteous before God), adopted as children of God, progressively sanctified by the Spirit into Christ's likeness, and will be finally glorified. Salvation is God's gift from first to last, received, not achieved. No part of this doctrine may be adjusted to make room for human contribution; the whole of Scripture's teaching on salvation excludes human boasting (Ephesians 2:9).

## Biblical Foundation

Ephesians 2:8-9 states the doctrine's foundation with unmistakable clarity: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). Every clause of this text is deliberate: salvation is by grace (its source), through faith (its means), not of yourselves (its origin is outside the sinner), the gift of God (its character), not of works (its exclusion of human merit), lest any man should boast (its purpose — that God alone receives the glory).

For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast. Ephesians 2:8-9

John 3:16 provides the second controlling text, locating salvation's ultimate source in the love of God and its means in simple faith: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life" (John 3:16). Romans 10:9-10 states the doctrine from the standpoint of the sinner's response: "That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation" (Romans 10:9-10). And Romans 5:1 states the immediate result of this faith: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 5:1). Together these texts establish salvation's source (grace), its ground (Christ's finished work), its means (faith), and its immediate fruit (peace with God through justification).

A fifth text confirms the scope and urgency of this offer. Paul writes to the Romans, "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek" (Romans 1:16). This text establishes salvation's universal offer — extended to every nation, without ethnic or social qualification — and its singular means: it comes only through believing the gospel, the good news of what Christ has already accomplished, never through any rival path.

For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. John 3:16
