days.title: Doctrine 9, Day 2: Biblical Development
days.content:
### The Old Testament Hope of the Day of the LORD

The Old Testament anticipates a decisive future day when God will act climactically in history — a day of judgment for the wicked and vindication for His people, repeatedly called "the day of the LORD." "The great day of the LORD is near, it is near, and hasteth greatly... That day is a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of wasteness and desolation" (Zephaniah 1:14-15), and yet also a day of restoration for the faithful: "the LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy" (Zephaniah 3:17). Joel foresees this day accompanied by the outpouring of God's Spirit, cosmic signs, and a call to "whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD" to "be delivered" (Joel 2:28-32). Obadiah announces the same day as universal in scope, "near upon all the heathen" (Obadiah 15), and Isaiah pictures it as the moment when every rival power, earthly and heavenly, is finally humbled before the true King: "the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously" (Isaiah 24:23) — judgment and the open reign of God arriving together, not as two separate events but as one act of the King reclaiming what is His.

The Old Testament also gives the doctrine's clearest early statement of bodily resurrection: "And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever" (Daniel 12:2-3). Job, amid great suffering, voices the same hope: "I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: and though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God" (Job 19:25-26). Isaiah closes his prophecy with the same forward horizon: "the LORD hath created a new thing in the earth" (Jeremiah 31:22) is echoed by Isaiah's own vision of "new heavens and a new earth" in which "the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind" (Isaiah 65:17), and Isaiah 25:8 promises that God "will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears off all faces" — language the New Testament will later take up directly (1 Corinthians 15:54; Revelation 21:4). Daniel 7:13-14 and 2:44, already cited in this chapter's introduction, add the certainty that God's kingdom will finally overtake and outlast every human empire, standing "for ever."

Other prophetic voices add further texture to this hope. Isaiah promises, "Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in dust: for thy dew is as the dew of herbs, and the earth shall cast out the dead" (Isaiah 26:19). Ezekiel is given a vision of a valley of dry bones, lifeless and scattered, which at the word of the LORD come together, are covered with flesh, and are filled with breath and stand "an exceeding great army" (Ezekiel 37:1-10) — a vision given directly to picture Israel's national restoration, yet resting on the same conviction the rest of the canon makes explicit: the LORD who can raise dry bones to life is the LORD who will raise the dead. Hosea voices the same defiant hope in briefer compass: "I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death: O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction" (Hosea 13:14) — language Paul will take up directly in his own resurrection chapter (1 Corinthians 15:55). And the Old Testament canon's final word on the coming day holds both judgment and healing together without contradiction: "the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven... But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings" (Malachi 4:1-2). Zechariah even names the geography of that day with striking specificity: "his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east... and the LORD shall be king over all the earth: in that day shall there be one LORD, and his name one" (Zechariah 14:4, 9) — the very location from which, centuries later, the angels would tell the watching disciples that the ascended Jesus would return "in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven" (Acts 1:11-12).

### Christ's Own Teaching on His Return

Jesus speaks of His own return repeatedly and without ambiguity. On the Mount of Olives, asked about "the sign of thy coming, and of the end of the world," He describes a coming that will be as unmistakable as lightning flashing from east to west: "then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory" (Matthew 24:3, 27, 30). He repeatedly presses the point that the exact timing is unknown even to Him in His incarnate state ("of that day and hour knoweth no man... but my Father only," Matthew 24:36), and therefore urges watchfulness rather than calculation: "Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come" (Matthew 24:42), reinforced by the parables of the ten virgins, the talents, and the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25), each ending in a reckoning before the returning King. The sheep and the goats especially name the shape of that final reckoning: "When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory: And before him shall be gathered all nations: and he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd divideth his sheep from the goats" (Matthew 25:31-32), the righteous entering "life eternal" and the unrighteous "everlasting punishment" (Matthew 25:46) — a judgment that is universal in scope ("all nations"), personal (Christ Himself presides), and final (there is no reversal named on either side). Earlier, the parable of the wheat and the tares makes the same point in miniature: both grow together until the harvest, "the end of the world," when the reapers, who are angels, will "gather out of his kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity," while "the righteous shall shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father" (Matthew 13:39-43) — present mixture, certain future separation. Luke records Jesus describing cosmic signs preceding His return, and then a command that reframes the whole subject away from dread: "when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh" (Luke 21:27-28) — for the believer, the doctrine's proper effect is hope, not terror.

Jesus is equally direct that the resurrection includes both the righteous and the unrighteous, though to opposite ends: "all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, and shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation" (John 5:28-29) — the same certainty of bodily resurrection applying to every person, with the outcome determined by their relationship to Him. Luke records the same summons to readiness in the language of household servants awaiting their master's return from a wedding: "Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning; and ye yourselves like unto men that wait for their lord... Blessed are those servants, whom the lord when he cometh shall find watching" (Luke 12:35-37) — a posture of active, working readiness, not idle anticipation.

In the upper room, Jesus grounds the disciples' hope in His own promise to return personally for them: "Let not your heart be troubled... I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also" (John 14:1-3). He also names Himself directly as the ground of resurrection hope: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (John 11:25), spoken at the tomb of Lazarus just before raising him — a preview, in history, of what He promises to do for all who are His at the last day (John 6:39-40, 44, 54, where Jesus repeats four times, "I will raise him up at the last day").

### The Apostolic Hope in Acts and the Epistles

The apostles preach Christ's return and the resurrection as central, load-bearing convictions, not peripheral speculation. At His ascension, as already noted, the angels promise His visible, bodily return (Acts 1:11). Paul devotes an entire chapter, 1 Corinthians 15, to the resurrection's certainty, reasoning that the believer's own future resurrection stands or falls with Christ's already-accomplished one: "if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen: And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain... And if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins. Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished... But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept" (1 Corinthians 15:13-14, 17-18, 20). The logic is deliberately airtight: because Christ genuinely rose — the "firstfruits," the first installment of a larger harvest still to come — everyone united to Him by faith is guaranteed to share the same resurrection He has already entered. His empty tomb is not simply proof of His own identity; it is, in the New Testament's own reasoning, the down payment guaranteeing every believer's future. He describes the resurrection body through the analogy of a planted seed: "that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die: And that which thou sowest, thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain... But God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him" (1 Corinthians 15:36-38) — continuity and transformation together, the seed and the plant genuinely connected yet the second far more glorious than the first. On this pattern the body is "sown in corruption," "raised in incorruption"; "sown in dishonour," "raised in glory"; "sown in weakness," "raised in power"; "sown a natural body," "raised a spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:42-44) — truly bodily, truly continuous with the body that died, yet transformed beyond its present limitations. He closes with the promise that "this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality... then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory" (1 Corinthians 15:53-54).

To a church grieving those who had died, Paul writes 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 precisely "that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope," grounding comfort in the certainty of the resurrection and Christ's personal return, and closing, "wherefore comfort one another with these words" (1 Thessalonians 4:18). He follows immediately with a call to sober readiness, since "the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2), urging believers to "watch and be sober" as "children of light" rather than being overtaken unaware (1 Thessalonians 5:4-8). Paul also anchors final judgment as a certainty for every person: "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad" (2 Corinthians 5:10), and elsewhere as a universal reckoning: "it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment" (Hebrews 9:27).

Paul writes similarly to the Philippians of a citizenship that is not finally earthly: "our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ: who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself" (Philippians 3:20-21) — the resurrection body is not a replacement of the old but its transformation, patterned after Christ's own risen body. He weighs present affliction against this coming glory and finds it no contest at all: "I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us" (Romans 8:18). John adds the doctrine's sanctifying effect: "it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is. And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure" (1 John 3:2-3) — right expectation of the end produces holiness now, not complacency. And Paul assures a persecuted church that final judgment will set every present injustice right: God will "recompense tribulation to them that trouble you," while granting "rest" to the afflicted, "when the Lord Jesus shall be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, in flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God, and that obey not the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ" (2 Thessalonians 1:6-8).

2 Peter addresses those who scoff at the promise of Christ's coming, insisting that the apparent delay is the LORD's patience, "not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance," and that "the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up" (2 Peter 3:9-10) — a decisive, purging judgment upon the present created order, followed immediately by the promise already cited: "we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness" (2 Peter 3:13). Titus 2:13 sums up the whole apostolic posture toward the future in a single phrase: believers live "looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ."

James counsels patient endurance modeled on the farmer awaiting harvest: "Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it... Stablish your hearts: for the coming of the Lord draweth nigh" (James 5:7-8), adding that "the judge standeth before the door" (James 5:9) as both warning and comfort. And near the end of his own life, Paul writes with the settled confidence this whole doctrine is meant to produce: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing" (2 Timothy 4:7-8) — eschatology, for the apostle facing death, is not abstract doctrine but present, sustaining hope.

### The Intermediate State

Between a believer's death and the final resurrection, Scripture is clear that the departed are not unconscious or annihilated but present, consciously, with the Lord. Paul describes his own confidence plainly: "we are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8), and facing the possibility of execution he writes, "having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better" than remaining in the body (Philippians 1:23). Jesus Himself promises the repentant thief crucified beside Him, on the very day of His own death, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43) — immediate presence with Christ, not a long, unconscious interval before some later arrival. The writer of Hebrews describes those already gathered around God's heavenly throne as "the spirits of just men made perfect" (Hebrews 12:23), and John, given a vision of martyrs already in heaven, hears them cry out, aware, remembering, and awaiting final justice (Revelation 6:9-10). This present, conscious fellowship with Christ, real and good as it is, is nevertheless not the doctrine's final word — the New Testament's hope is not merely a disembodied intermediate state but the bodily resurrection still to come, when what is now "absent from the body" is reunited, transformed and glorified, exactly as Christ's own body was raised.

### The Consummation in Revelation

Revelation brings the whole canon's eschatological hope to its climax. Christ is revealed as the conquering King, riding out on a white horse, "KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS," to judge and make war in righteousness, with the armies of heaven following Him (Revelation 19:11-16) — the decisive, visible end of every rebellion against His reign. Revelation 20 describes Satan bound and cast down, "that he should deceive the nations no more" for a time, and then, at the end, "loosed a little season" before his final doom, "cast into the lake of fire and brimstone... tormented day and night for ever and ever" (Revelation 20:1-3, 7-10) — the certain, final undoing of the enemy this course's fourth book will treat at length. The chapter describes a resurrection of the righteous to reign with Christ (Revelation 20:4-6), and then a final, universal resurrection and judgment before "a great white throne," where "the dead, small and great, stand before God," and "the books were opened," and all are "judged... according to their works" (Revelation 20:11-13). Those whose names are not found written in the book of life face "the second death," everlasting separation from God (Revelation 20:14-15) — the certain, sobering reality Scripture calls the unrepentant to escape while grace remains (2 Thessalonians 1:8-9; Matthew 25:41, 46).

For the redeemed, the outcome is the opposite: everlasting joy in God's unveiled presence. Revelation 21-22 describes the new heaven and new earth already cited — no more death, sorrow, crying, or pain; the tabernacle of God with men; the LORD's own declaration, "It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely" (Revelation 21:6); a city whose light is the glory of God and the Lamb, needing no sun (Revelation 21:23); a river of the water of life and a tree of life bearing continual fruit for the healing of the nations (Revelation 22:1-2), and "his servants shall serve him: and they shall see his face; and his name shall be in their foreheads... and they shall reign for ever and ever" (Revelation 22:3-5). Even amid the book's severe visions of judgment, a voice from heaven pronounces a benediction over those who die in the faith: "Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them" (Revelation 14:13) — the same comfort Paul gave the Thessalonians, sounded again from heaven itself. Christ's own closing word to the book, and to the whole canon, is a promise: "Behold, I come quickly; and my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be" (Revelation 22:12). The book, and the canon, close with the church's own answering prayer to this certain hope: "Even so, come, Lord Jesus" (Revelation 22:20).

### A Renewed Creation, Not an Abandoned One

It is worth stating plainly what this consummation is not. It is not the annihilation of the material world in favor of a purely spiritual, disembodied eternity. Revelation's own language resists that reading: the redeemed possess resurrection bodies, not merely liberated souls; the setting is a city and a garden, with a river, trees, fruit, and light, not an abstraction; and John explicitly sees a new earth, not the absence of one (Revelation 21:1). Even 2 Peter's severe language of the present heavens and earth being "dissolved" and "burned up" (2 Peter 3:10-12) is followed immediately, in the very next breath, by the promise of "new heavens and a new earth" (2 Peter 3:13) — judgment by fire purifying and remaking, on the pattern of purification already familiar from Scripture's other refining images (Malachi 3:2-3; 1 Corinthians 3:13-15), not judgment erasing creation from existence altogether. The one detail Revelation names as absent from the new earth — "there was no more sea" (Revelation 21:1) — trades on the sea's ancient biblical association with chaos and threat (Psalm 74:13-14; Job 38:8-11), not a claim that literal bodies of water vanish; its removal signals that every remaining source of disorder, danger, and separation is gone. What Doctrine 7 named as a very good creation, corrupted by sin and groaning for release, is here shown to be restored, not replaced — the consistent pattern of Scripture's redemption, which heals and glorifies what sin has broken rather than discarding it.

### The Certainty of Final Separation from God

Scripture states with equal plainness that this glorious future is not the destination of every person. Jesus Himself speaks of a final separation in the starkest terms He uses anywhere in His teaching, describing those who refused to show mercy as departing "into everlasting punishment," set opposite "the righteous into life eternal" in the very same sentence (Matthew 25:46), and He warns, in His own words, of a place "where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched" (Mark 9:43-48), urging the most drastic measures to avoid it rather than presuming upon it. John records the same certainty in the plainest possible terms of present standing: "He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him" (John 3:36) — the outcome is not undecided or merely probable; it rests, even now, on one's relationship to the Son. Paul describes this destiny as "everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power" (2 Thessalonians 1:9), and Revelation, as already shown, names it "the second death" for all whose names are not written in the book of life (Revelation 20:14-15; 21:8). This course states this reality because Scripture states it plainly, not to speculate beyond what is written; its intended effect, throughout the New Testament, is never idle curiosity but urgent, compassionate appeal — exactly the use Paul makes of it when he immediately follows his own account of the judgment seat of Christ with the confession, "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men" (2 Corinthians 5:10-11).

### The Believer's Works and the Judgment Seat of Christ

Scripture distinguishes the believer's certain, settled salvation from a further reckoning still to come — an evaluation of what has been built upon that salvation's foundation. Paul describes every believer's works as building material laid upon "the foundation... Jesus Christ," material that will be tested "by fire; and the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is" (1 Corinthians 3:11-13). Work that endures the test receives reward; work that does not is "burned," yet the builder himself "shall be saved; yet so as by fire" (1 Corinthians 3:14-15) — salvation itself is never in question for the one in Christ, but the substance of a life lived for Him is. This is the same reckoning Paul has in view when he writes, "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad" (2 Corinthians 5:10), and again, "every one of us shall give account of himself to God" (Romans 14:12).

This future accounting is meant to shape present labor rather than produce present anxiety. Paul urges believers to build wisely now, since the day itself "shall declare it" (1 Corinthians 3:13), and John exhorts continued abiding in Christ "that, when he shall appear, we may have confidence, and not be ashamed before him at his coming" (1 John 2:28). Christ Himself promises that "every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour" (1 Corinthians 3:8), and pictures faithful stewardship rewarded with greater trust in His kingdom: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant... enter thou into the joy of thy lord" (Matthew 25:21). The certainty of this reckoning is meant to press every believer toward faithfulness, not fear — a servant who already belongs to the Master, giving account of how that belonging has been lived out.

### Watchfulness Against Deception

Alongside the certainty of Christ's return, Scripture repeatedly warns that the interval before it will be marked by deception, and that believers are to meet this danger with sober discernment rather than either panic or careless speculation. Jesus' own Olivet discourse begins its description of the last days with this warning first, before any other sign: "Take heed that no man deceive you. For many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ; and shall deceive many" (Matthew 24:4-5), and He repeats it again near the same discourse's center: "there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect" (Matthew 24:24). Paul gives the same caution to a church anxious about the timing of Christ's return, urging them not to be "soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand," warning that a great falling away and the revealing of a great lawless figure must first occur (2 Thessalonians 2:1-3) — Scripture's own corrective against every premature claim that the end has already arrived. John likewise warns a church facing false teaching that "even now are there many antichrists," and counsels, "believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God" (1 John 2:18; 4:1). This course does not adjudicate the disputed particulars of that interval's exact sequence; it states plainly what Scripture states plainly — that deception will come, that it will often claim Christ's own name and authority, and that believers are called to sober testing of every claim against the settled Word rather than credulous alarm at every new report.

### The Gospel to All Nations and the End

Scripture ties the timing of the end directly to the completion of the church's mission rather than presenting the two as unrelated. Jesus states the connection plainly in His own Olivet discourse: "this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come" (Matthew 24:14) — the church's ongoing task of proclamation is not incidental background to the end but bound up with it. Peter gives the same connection from the opposite angle, explaining an apparent delay in Christ's return as itself an expression of divine patience rather than divine slowness: the Lord is "longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance" (2 Peter 3:9) — the interval before the end is itself mercy, extending opportunity for the gospel to reach still more of the nations.

Revelation supplies the completed picture this mission is working toward: a "great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues," standing before the throne and before the Lamb, crying, "Salvation to our God which sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb" (Revelation 7:9-10). This is not a picture eschatology merely observes from a distance; it is the very outcome the church's mission, traced at length in Doctrine 8, is laboring toward now. The certain end and the church's present sending are, in this sense, two sides of a single divine purpose — the same King who has fixed the day has also appointed the means by which the nations come to know Him before it arrives (Romans 10:14-15).

### Every Knee Shall Bow: Christ's Kingship Acknowledged at the End

The end this doctrine traces is not merely the removal of evil but the open, universal acknowledgment of a kingship that has been true all along, even while the nations denied or ignored it. The Psalter already anticipates this outcome in the LORD's own address to His anointed King: "Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession" (Psalm 2:8), a decree the nations are warned to heed "lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way" (Psalm 2:12). Revelation shows this inheritance finally taken up in full: the returning Christ "shall rule them with a rod of iron," His title inscribed for every eye to see — "KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS" (Revelation 19:15-16) — the same royal claim Daniel had foreseen given "dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him" (Daniel 7:14), now openly and finally exercised.

Paul describes this same universal acknowledgment as the appointed destination of Christ's own humiliation and exaltation: because He "humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross," God has "highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father" (Philippians 2:8-11). This confession will not be forced from the reluctant only; it is the whole creation's rightful, appointed response to the King who made it, redeemed a people from it, and is coming to claim it fully — the same claim this chapter opened with in Daniel 2:44, now brought at last to its unshakable, everlasting fulfillment.

days.title: Doctrine 9, Day 3: Christ Revealed
days.content:
Christ Revealed Eschatology reveals Christ as the returning King and righteous Judge — the same Jesus who ascended will descend, this time not in humility but "in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory" (Matthew 24:30), and "the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son" (John 5:22), so that "the Lord, the righteous judge" will render to each what is due at "that day" (2 Timothy 4:8). Abraham had long ago appealed to God as "the Judge of all the earth," confident He would "do right" (Genesis 18:25); Paul's preaching at Athens names exactly who that Judge finally is: God "hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead" (Acts 17:31) — the resurrection itself is God's own public guarantee of who will judge, and that the judgment is certain. He is revealed as the resurrection and the life in person, not merely the teacher of a doctrine about resurrection — "I am the resurrection, and the life" (John 11:25) — so that the hope of every believer's own rising is inseparable from union with Him, the "firstfruits of them that slept" (1 Corinthians 15:20). When John himself sees the risen and glorified Christ, he falls "at his feet as dead," and Christ's own self-description settles, once and for all, who holds authority over the grave: "Fear not; I am the first and the last: I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death" (Revelation 1:17-18). Death itself is under His hand, not the reverse. And He is revealed as the one who personally makes all things new: "he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new" (Revelation 21:5), the same voice that first spoke light out of darkness now speaking a whole creation into its final, glorious order. The end of all things, no less than the beginning, belongs to Him.

This is why eschatology, rightly taught, never becomes mere speculation about timelines. Its center is a person, not a chart — the same Christ who died and rose is the one who is coming again, and every certain element of this doctrine is certain because it rests on His own word and His own accomplished resurrection, "the firstfruits" guaranteeing the harvest to follow.

days.title: Doctrine 9, Day 4: Kingdom Implications
days.content:
Eschatology is the kingdom's guaranteed destination, and that guarantee shapes how the church understands its present labor. Because Christ's kingdom is certain to be finally and fully established, the church's present mission is neither futile nor merely provisional busywork; it is meaningful, kingdom-building labor whose fruit is secured by the King who is coming to claim it. "Be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 15:58) — a verse that follows directly on Paul's resurrection chapter for exactly this reason.

Eschatology also confirms that evil, however entrenched it may presently appear, does not have the final word. Satan's doom, death's defeat, and every hostile power's subjection are certain outcomes, already guaranteed in Christ's resurrection and awaiting only their full unveiling (1 Corinthians 15:24-26; Revelation 20:10). And it confirms that God's justice, so often deferred or denied in this present age, will be perfectly and finally rendered — no wrong ultimately unaddressed, no faithful suffering ultimately unseen, "for God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil" (Ecclesiastes 12:14). The kingdom that began in creation and now advances visibly through the church will not stall short of its goal; it will be delivered complete into the Father's hands (1 Corinthians 15:24), and "the kingdoms of this world" will finally "become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever" (Revelation 11:15).

This also clarifies the relationship between the kingdom's present and future forms traced across this whole chapter. The kingdom is genuinely present now — inaugurated in Christ's first coming, embodied visibly in His church, exercised wherever His Word is obeyed and His gospel proclaimed. Yet it is not yet complete; sin, suffering, and death remain real, and the creation Doctrine 7 described as groaning has not yet been delivered into "the glorious liberty of the children of God" (Romans 8:21). Eschatology holds these two truths together without collapsing either into the other: the church labors now under a King who reigns already, and it labors in confident hope of a King who is coming to finish what He has begun. Neither presumption that the kingdom has fully arrived nor despair that it has not truly come at all does justice to what Scripture actually teaches.

This also confirms that the new heavens and new earth are the true destination of the whole biblical story traced across this chapter, not a departure from it. Doctrine 7 began with a good creation, groaning under the weight of human sin yet never abandoned by its Maker; Doctrine 9 ends with that same creation renewed, not discarded — the tabernacle of God finally and permanently "with men" on a redeemed earth (Revelation 21:3), the curse lifted (Revelation 22:3), and a garden's original purpose fulfilled forever (Revelation 22:1-2). The Bible's story does not end with redeemed souls evacuated from a ruined world; it ends with God making all things new. Creation's opening claim in Genesis 1:1 and eschatology's closing vision in Revelation 21-22 are, in this sense, one continuous act of the same King.

This certain future also gives content to a prayer believers already pray. When Christ taught His disciples to pray, "Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:10), He was not teaching them to ask for something uncertain or merely hoped-for. He was teaching them to ask, with confidence, for the very thing this doctrine has traced as certain — the full and final arrival of what has already been inaugurated in Christ and is even now advancing through His church. Every believer who prays those words is asking, whether they know it or not, for Revelation 21 and 22 to arrive.

The certainty of a coming reckoning for every believer's works also shapes the kingdom's present labor. Because the King who is coming will evaluate what has been built on the foundation He has already laid (1 Corinthians 3:11-15), no faithful service rendered to Him in obscurity is wasted or forgotten, and no kingdom labor is finally hidden from the eyes of the One it was rendered to. And because the interval before His return is marked by real deception, often wearing His own name, the kingdom's advance depends on a church that tests every claim to speak for the King against His own settled Word, rather than one swept along by whatever voice speaks most urgently of His imminent return.

The certainty that every knee will one day bow and every tongue confess Christ as Lord (Philippians 2:10-11) also settles, in advance, any question of whether the present rebellion of the nations against their rightful King is permanent. It is not. The same reversal this chapter traced from Daniel's vision of a kingdom that would "stand for ever" (Daniel 2:44) is guaranteed to reach its full, visible, universal conclusion — not a hope contingent on human progress, but a certainty resting on the Father's own decree to His Son (Psalm 2:8) and already sealed by the resurrection (Acts 17:31).

days.title: Doctrine 9, Day 5: Practical Implications
days.content:
Living This Out Let the certainty of Christ's return produce watchfulness, not speculation — refuse to set dates or chase timelines Scripture does not give, and instead "watch" in readiness as He commanded (Matthew 24:36, 42). Comfort those who grieve believing loved ones with the resurrection hope, "that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13-18). Live soberly and expectantly as a "child of light," not surprised or unprepared "as a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:4-8). Let the certainty of final judgment sharpen urgency in evangelism — every person will stand before God, and the gospel is the only remedy (2 Corinthians 5:10-11, 20). Persevere in present labor for the kingdom, confident that nothing done in obedience to Christ is wasted, however small or unseen it seems now (1 Corinthians 15:58). Let the hope of resurrection and Christ's appearing produce present purity, not present indifference — "every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself" (1 John 3:3). Find real comfort amid present suffering by weighing it against what is coming, without minimizing the pain of the present moment (Romans 8:18; 2 Corinthians 4:17). Build your life's labor with care, remembering that it will be tested and that faithful service, however small or unnoticed now, receives its own reward from the King (1 Corinthians 3:12-14; Matthew 25:21). Test every claim to speak for Christ, especially claims about His return, against the settled Word rather than accepting them on the strength of urgency or apparent signs alone (1 John 4:1; 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3). Live even now in light of the day when every knee will bow to Christ, letting that certainty humble present pride and steady present fear alike (Philippians 2:10-11). Support the church's mission to the nations as inseparable from the timing of Christ's own return, recognizing that gospel proclamation and eschatological hope are not two separate concerns but one (Matthew 24:14).

None of this hope is meant to produce escapism, passivity, or morbid fascination with prophetic detail at the expense of present obedience. Scripture consistently pairs eschatological certainty with a summons to holy, active, hopeful living now — not "gazing up into heaven" in idle wonder (Acts 1:11), but working, watching, and witnessing until the same Jesus returns.

Every certainty this doctrine has traced — the return, the resurrection, the judgment, the new creation, the bowed knee of every nation — is meant to be held the same way the apostles held it: not as abstract information to master, but as present hope strong enough to steady fear, sharpen urgency, and settle the heart until the King appears.

days.title: Doctrine 9, Day 6: Summary
days.content: Summary Jesus Christ will return visibly, bodily, and personally in power and glory. The dead will be raised; all people will stand before God in final judgment; the redeemed will enter everlasting joy in God's presence in the new heavens and new earth, and the unrepentant will face everlasting separation from Him. History is moving toward the full and final establishment of God's kingdom, not toward nothing and not toward mere human progress. This is eschatology's certain core, whatever genuine breadth remains among believers over its particular sequence and timing. Creation began the kingdom's story; the church carries the kingdom's present witness; and the return of Christ brings the kingdom to its appointed, glorious end — the King who made all things and redeemed a people for Himself coming again to make all things new, and to reign for ever and ever.

doctrines.title: Angelology
doctrines.summary: The doctrine of angels — created spirits who worship God and serve the heirs of salvation

days.title: Doctrine 10, Day 1: Overview & Biblical Foundation
days.content:
Scripture assumes, rather than argues for, the existence of an entire order of created beings distinct from both God and humanity: the angels. They appear at nearly every major turning point in the biblical narrative — guarding Eden, announcing covenant promises, delivering the Law, strengthening prophets, announcing the incarnation, ministering to Christ, rolling away the stone, and gathering the elect at the last day. They are never presented as myth, symbol, or literary device. They are presented as real, personal, created spirit beings who exist for the glory and service of God and who minister, under His command, to the heirs of salvation.

This doctrine matters because a biblical worldview is larger than the visible world. Scripture insists that "by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers" (Colossians 1:16). To understand angels rightly is to understand something true about the size, order, and worship of the universe Christ made and rules — and to be recalled, every time, to the fact that angels themselves point away from themselves and toward Him.

## Biblical Foundation

Four passages anchor this doctrine. Psalm 103:20-21 describes angels as mighty ones who "excel in strength, that do his commandments, hearkening unto the voice of his word," who "do his pleasure" as His ministers. Hebrews 1:14 asks and answers the defining question of angelic purpose: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?" Colossians 1:16 establishes their origin: they are created beings, "thrones... dominions... principalities... powers," made by and for Christ. And Revelation 5:11-12 shows their true posture before the throne — an innumerable company encircling the Lamb, crying with a loud voice that He is worthy to receive power, riches, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing.

These four texts together establish the doctrine's shape: angels are created, they are powerful, they are obedient, their purpose is to serve God's will and God's people, and their highest activity is not service but worship. Any biblical teaching on angels that loses sight of these four anchors — createdness, power under command, ministry to believers, and worship of Christ — has drifted from the text.

It is worth pausing on what each anchor text rules out as much as what it establishes. Psalm 103 rules out the idea that angels act on their own initiative or authority; they "do his commandments," full stop. Hebrews 1:14 rules out the idea that angelic ministry exists for its own sake; it exists "for them who shall be heirs of salvation" — angels serve believers, not the reverse. Colossians 1:16 rules out any notion that angels, however exalted their rank, stand outside the category of "created"; whatever a "throne" or "principality" may be in the unseen order, it was made by Christ and for Christ, exactly as everything else was. And Revelation 5:11-12 rules out any suggestion that angels compete with the Lamb for glory; the innumerable company exists, in that scene, entirely to ascribe worth to another. Read together, these texts leave no room for angels as independent spiritual agents to be courted, feared apart from God's sovereignty, or treated as a parallel channel of divine power distinct from Christ Himself.
